speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce, with some satisfaction, that a problem that has confronted Canada for the past several weeks seems to have been resolved.

subtopic: PACIFIC COAST LONGSHOREMEN DISPUTE-AGREEMENT TO RETURN TO WORK
speechtext:
I might add that it has been resolved only within the last five minutes. The tie-up, which has paralysed the ports of British Columbia for the past several days and which is now having such far-reaching adverse affects, has not only been a matter of serious concern to members of this house but also one of serious concern to the stevedoring companies and to the union employees involved. Each of them state that they have a certain position to maintain. But in view of the tie-up of grain, lumber and other forest products, and of other water-borne products, in response to an appeal that I made on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and which was concurred in by the premier of British Columbia, they have agreed to an acceptance in principle of the formula which I proposed to them over the week end, with one further condition, namely that the Minister of Labour will set up an industrial inquiry commission to inquire into the cause of this work stoppage, with a view to making recommendations that might prevent further stoppages of this nature, including the undertaking that one of the parties has agreed upon and which is acceptable to the other side. In addition the undertaking on the part of the employers concerned will be one of the items that will be considered by the industrial inquiry commission.
I have received a proposal in writing from one side. I have received an answering wire from the other side, but certain supplementary clauses have to be added to that wire. I understand it will be dispatched within the next few minutes, but it is expected that work will resume in all west coast ports within a matter of hours.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: GRAIN-MEETING OF COMMITTEE TO CO-ORDINATE MOVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of, among other things, the large scale back-up of wheat and other grains on the prairies as the result of the strike in Vancouver, and the importance of moving it to markets with all possible expedition, now that the labour difficulties have been resolved, I wish to inform the house, on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and myself, that the Pacific grain transportation committee will be reconvened.
The government is pleased that the committee will once again meet under the chairmanship of Mr. William Riddell, former assistant chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, who acted so successfully in this capacity for several months early this year.
The function of the committee will be to co-ordinate the movement of grain to ensure that shipments are put back on schedule as quickly as possible. The Minister of Transport and I are confident that all of the companies and the many workers involved will play their part in ensuring a maximum movement of grain. I have no doubt that this co-operative approach to a challenging task will once again be successful, and that the Wheat Board's commitments from the west coast will be fully met.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say in respect of Bill C-227. I think the discussion in the house on this medical care bill was very fruitful. It brought out ideas, particularly in the field of paramedical services, by pointing out the role played in the field of medical care by optometrists, physiotherapists, podiatrists, psychologists and other allied services. I think this was very beneficial. I believe the minister would be the first to admit this.
I do not intend to dwell too long on this point. The minister, introduced an amendment which indicated that he was not entirely averse to suggestions made to him by this party. We appreciate this co-operation. As the house will recall, I moved an amendment to the effect that there be at least a partial medical care plan effective July 1, 1967, which would cover at least 30 per cent of the people across this land who are not otherwise covered and who have difficulty in respect of their medical bills. Having said this, I find myself in a quandary and in a very difficult position with regard to the delay in the date for implementation of this bill. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) says that it is a question of priorities. So far as I am concerned, those priorities were not fully defined.
How in the world can the minister say to the house now that he will not be in a position to implement this measure on July 1, 1967 but come what may he will be in a position to do so on July 1, 1968. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is not a positive type of thinking. How in the world is he going to know more about the economy on July 1, 1968, than he will know on July 1, 1967? I think this puzzles every member of this house. Here we are, after five years of unprecedented prosperity. We have had the largest wheat sales in the history of this country. These sales amounted to over $1 billion last year. Our pulp and forest production is at an alltime high. How in the world can the minister tell us what the situation will be on July 1, 1968? How can he make such statements now, after we have had five years of prosperity such as this country has never known before? I reiterate that surely he knows his position better in 1967 than he will know it in 1968.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand):
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that consideration be given to amending it by striking out "1st day of July 1968" in line 9 of paragraph 2(b) thereof, and substituting "1st day of July 1967".

I think it will be agreed by all parties in the house that improvements were made to the bill because of the persistence with which those points were pressed. There is no question but that the bill as it stands now before us is a better bill than it was when it was introduced.
I suggest that this house should carry on with its good work by improving this bill still further and that the government should pay the same attention to this request, that the act come into force on July 1, 1967, that it paid to some of the other matters presented to it from this side of the house. At first, the minister resisted the requests from this side of the house that the scope of the coverage be enlarged, but in due course he not only agreed to that idea but also had the pleasure of introducing an amendment to that effect. I suggest he should take the same attitude in respect of the matter which is before the house now. I consider we are doing him a service in giving him an opportunity to go back to the date originally planned, namely, July 1, 1967.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), in speaking to this matter of the date
December 8, 1966

when we were in committee of the whole on the bill, made what I am sure everyone recognized as an excellent case against the arguments advanced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) for postponing the adoption of medicare by one year.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
As a matter of fact, all of the arguments that the minister used really have no weight. One must consider the fact that medicare does not involve a great increase in the total amount of money to be spent by the community as a whole on medical costs. To a large extent it involves a rechannelling of the moneys that are already being spent. It is also true that some of the provinces may not be ready to come in right at the start. Therefore, when one adds all these factors together it becomes clear that to bring this legislation into effect on July 1, 1967 would not have any appreciable inflationary effect.
That argument having been squashed, it seems to me that the government ought to reconsider its position. If there is a recorded vote on this amendment and the government resists it, in those circumstances if it is carried there will be a parliamentary crisis. But the government does not need to take that position. The government has already accepted suggestions from the opposition side of the house. I suggest, therefore, what it should do now is to accept this last minute suggestion that we go back to the date which was originally promised by the government.
Let me point out also that the need for medicare in this country is very real and that there are many people week by week and month by month who are faced with medical costs or needs they cannot have attended to because of the cost. We are being unfair and inhuman in postponing a plan, the principles of which we have accepted. For the sake of the people of this country and their needs, if we have something here that is good and we all now agree in that regard on all sides of the house, let us not postpone it for another 18 or 19 months when it is within our power to have it come into effect on Canada's 100th birthday, next July 1.
Another point I wish to refer to is the fact that I still think there is importance in political parties keeping their promises. There is no promise better known to the Canadian people, because it has been around for such a long time, than the promise of the Liberals in 1919 to bring in health insurance or medicare. Despite the fact that that promise, over several decades, was not implemented, the same
Medicare
party-the Liberal party-in the election campaign a year ago called on the Canadian people to believe, in spite of all its failures in the past, that this time it was serious and would keep its word. The Liberals asked the people to believe that medicare would be brought into effect on the date of that promise, July 1, 1967.
We play fast and loose with the whole political and democratic process when these promises are so lightly set aside. I feel, therefore, that instead of the government making it necessary to have a prolonged debate and making it necessary for this issue to be decided by a recorded vote-if it is not accepted we will have a recorded vote-it should do as it did on the question of extending coverage, agree that this is a good idea and accept this amendment so we can go back into the committee of the whole to improve this bill in this one more particular.
I commend the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) on producing this amendment. As I said, I had one worded in a slightly different fashion but for the same purpose. I hope the house as a whole will agree with the two of us who have already spoken, that we should now complete the job of making this a good bill by making its effective date July 1, 1967.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak for a moment about the financial aspects surrounding the introduction of this bill on July 1, 1968. The effective date of this measure has been put off for one year, but not for any medical reason. We all know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) was most anxious that it should be effective on July 1, 1967. It is being postponed because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) suggests the country will be better able financially to implement this measure one year later.
I disagree very strongly with the Minister of Finance, because it is my belief we will be far better able from a financial point of view to implement this bill on July 1, 1967 than a year later. I believe that for these reasons: It is easy to see by examining the financial and economic conditions of this country at this time and comparing them with the circumstances which existed ten years ago this month that the circumstances are the same.
In December of 1956, we were reaching the end of six years of unprecedented prosperity. At that time the government became alarmed about the effects of inflation, as it is today,

December 8. 1966'
Medicare
and imposed a tight money policy upon the country. Six months later in spite of a strong warning by the government economic adviser, Dr. Firestone, the country was plunged into a serious recession, and it took three years to pull the country out of that recession.
The country is in exactly the same position today and all one has to do to understand that is examine any of the economic indicators which reveal our economic health. A tight money policy was imposed on this country about one year ago. Dr. Firestone advised the government a number of months ago that if it did not change its monetary policy the same thing which happened ten years ago would happen again.

I was quoting the amendment which we moved. It reads further:
This house, while of the opinion that provision should be made for medical services to be available to all Canadians at an adequate level on a prepaid basis, is nevertheless of the further opinion that no legislation for the provision of insured medical care services in Canada will be satisfactory unless it:
(a)	secures co-operation of the governments of the provinces of Canada;
(b)	recognizes the principle of voluntary choice by the individual;
(c)	makes adequate prior provision for sufficient medical research, the training of adequate numbers of doctors and other medical personnel, and;
December 8, 1966

(d)	Immediately provides for those persons who are unable, for financial reasons, to provide medical services for themselves.
So, the amendment we moved came within all four principles of the enunciated policy. The government found it necessary to change the undertaking given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). For 47 years, the Liberal party promised health insurance. For 47 years, during every election, it undertook to bring the legislation into effect. The Prime Minister gave a clear undertaking to the Canadian people when he stated that this legislation would be brought into effect on July 1, 1967.
That the excuse for the postponement is the inflationary trend in this country has been answered by hon. gentlemen who have spoken. There is no possible excuse for the government to flout its undertakings. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) is one to which the minister, if he were true to the principles he enunciated before the rug was pulled from under him by the Prime Minister, could give complete support.
There are many people who need medicare. There was a statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) which was entirely applicable to the situation. To use his words: "Too many Canadians live in the shadow of the fear of crushing medical expenditures". These numerous Canadians will be asked to wait a further year from July 1, 1967. The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) has expressed his idea of the reason for this unexplained and grossly improper repudiation of the pledged word of the Prime Minister and all with whom he is associated.
Parliament has been criticized. It should be criticized when ministers and leaders of parties make promises and undertakings, and then openly and without shame depart from them. The undertaking was clear and unequivocal. Our attitude was that the promise would not be carried into effect. It was a departure from many of the principles of the Hall commission and, in addition, was based on a declaration by the government that either the provinces accept the four principles enunciated by the Prime Minister or there would be no medicare available to them.
This matter falls exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces. In the debate that has taken place, tribute can be paid to many hon. members but I think there are two or three who deserve special mention: one is the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard), who moved the amendment in question today,
Medicare
the other is the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand), and the third is the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), not to mention others. The three hon. members I mentioned devoted themselves to bringing about changes in the government plan which the government finally found necessary to accept.
This is the purpose of parliament. Ministers who take the position of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), and who stubbornly oppose amendments without regard to the benefits which flow from them do not understand parliament. However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) did and he accepted various suggestions which were first regarded as essentially heretical. As the debate went on for five or six days, the government was forced to bring about changes. Public opinion enjoined the government to change its attitude and take account of the views expressed by Canadians in every part of this country, particularly those in the dental and medical professions, the optometrists, chiropractors, and so on. If the legislation had been rushed through in a couple of days, none of the ancillary professions would have received any consideration and none of the changes which have been brought about would have been achieved. This was parliament at its best. Hon. members should stand up and speak up, regardless of the stubbornness of the government in refusing to make changes.
I do not think that some of the amendments go as far as they have been interpreted. I think many of these professions to which I have referred, ancillary to the medical profession, will find in the implementation of the amendments agreed to, there are loopholes which will deny them the consideration which they expect. The matter is left to the provinces. It is the provinces which should determine which professions shall come within the ambit of medicare. Again, may I repeat that while advances have been made through the arguments which were placed before the house there is a possibility that the amendments agreed to will be found, on examination and implementation, to be not as comprehensive as some anticipate.
The amendment which we now move strikes at the heart of the problem which faces Canadians today, namely, respect for parliament. How can there be respect if a government commits an undertaking, advertises it and then produces a specious excuse to postpone the implementation of the promise? The reason which the government advances

December 8, 1966
Medicare
for the postponement is the inflationary trend. The fact remains that the government departs from its undertaking.

There may be hope, even yet, for redemption on the part of this government. I would go so far as to say that if the minister would permit a free vote on this question, allowing members who sit behind him to cast their vote free of the whip on the understanding that any adverse vote would not be regarded as a vote of non-confidence, he would find that members who speak their views outside the house would join with the opposition in bringing about the attainment of this legislation without making the people of Canada wait for 18 or 19 months.
I can only believe, Mr. Speaker, that the reason, or one of the reasons, for this postponement is that the government knows the plan will not work in its present form. Three provinces only have undertaken to apply it in its present form. The government is assured that the provinces will not accept direction by the federal government as to what they should do in matters peculiarly within their own jurisdiction. That being so, the government would postpone the date of implementation hoping that in the meantime something will happen to make it possible for them to alter the present bill and in co-operation with the provinces bring about legislation that will be effective.
In this way, Mr. Speaker, instead of this legislation merely being placed on the statute book as a postponed declaration of intention, it will be carried into effect.
The acceptance of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Simcoe East will be widely approved in every part of the country. This is what the people want. They want legislation that is effective. As far as the present legislation is concerned, I predict the government knows now that in its present form it cannot be effective. It might be had there been fuller consultation and agreement with the provinces. If this legislation were made effective now Canadians as a whole would realize that the government believes in carrying out its solemn undertakings, and that the flouting of its pledged word will not be tolerated by its supporters.

The more I study the statement made by the Minister of Finance the other night the more I am persuaded that there is some other reason for the postponement by one year of the effective date of this legislation, a reason that the Minister of Finance has simply not disclosed to parliament.
Every reason that the minister has given, Mr. Speaker, does not stand up to analysis from any point of view. As a matter of fact, the statement he made today that the money supply in the country has just been increased is surely the clearest indication that the Minister of Finance has joined the economic council in the belief that we are more in danger of a levelling off, or indeed of a going down, of our economy than we are of inflationary pressures at the present time. There

is, therefore, no excuse whatever for the postponement by a further year of the implementation of the medicare plan.
When 1 spoke on this matter the other night I aroused the ire of the Minister of Finance, as hon. members who were present will recall, when I suggested that I thought the Minister of Finance had responded to pressures from lobbies with special interests rather than sticking by the promise of his government to the Canadian people. I have studied economics throughout my life and I cannot see the slightest validity to any of the alleged reasons given by the Minister of Finance for postponing this legislation.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we are running the risk of the contrary happening. If it is true, as it obviously is, that the rate of growth of the economy is levelling off and the probability is that there will be some sort of dip-I hope a very small dip-in the expansion curve, the likelihood is that the implementation of this plan in 1968 will be a great deal more difficult than it would be in 1967.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
There is certainly nothing in the economic picture which would justify the government in saying it would be easier to implement this plan in 1968 than in 1967. On the contrary, I urge the government to see that a tax, or whatever is necessary to raise revenues in order to implement this plan, would be acceptable. A tax imposed for a specific and definite purpose from which everybody in Canada would benefit is not a tax which the people would resent or oppose. As one member of this house-and I speak for all the members of my party-I believe that honesty impels us to say that the introduction of a medicare plan of this sort will mean raising the necessary revenues, federally and provincially, by various tax measures. Nobody in Canada expects to get these benefits for nothing. We do not expect the minister to supply them for nothing. The people of Canada are prepared, however, to transfer the payments which they presently make directly to doctors or group plans, to another fund through the medium of tax payments.
There would be an important difference. Instead of people having to pay their medical bills when they are sick, and can least afford to do so, their bills would be paid automatically; and instead of the payments being made initially on the same basis by the poor as by the rich, the graduated scale of income tax, which I hope would be used as a means of raising this revenue, would mean that those
Medicare
who could afford to pay more would do so in order that poor people would get a medical service without having to pay as much for it as would otherwise be the case, or, indeed, without having to pay anything at all.
This is as easy to do in 1967 as it is likely to be in 1968. Indeed, if the economic situation should take a downward turn, 1968 might easily be a more difficult year. The Minister of National Health and Welfare had, if I may say so, the intelligence and the graciousness to accept urgings from this side of the house that he should give himself a greater degree of flexibility to expand medical services as the provinces expand them, on the authority of the Governor General in Council. This was what my leader, the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) suggested in an amendment he moved some days ago.
I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) without, I hope, any partisan undertones or overtones, to look at this amendment in the same way. Even if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) honestly believed in September last that the Canadian economic situation required a postponement-and I just cannot accept that he could have believed it-I say to the minister and to the government that the advice of the Economic Council, the indications of every economic index one can read, and even the evidence of the Minister of Finance today that the money supply has been increased, underline the fact that there is no longer any reason for postponement, even if three months ago there was one.
I think it would bring to the government of the day, as well as parliament itself, a great deal of credit if hon. gentlemen opposite were flexible enough to accept this amendment and were prepared to carry out the promise which they originally made. The other night the Minister of Finance talked about priorities. He had the new old-age supplementary assistance law to deal with; he had the Canada assistance plan to deal with. He intended to do these things one year, and the other things the second year.
I do not follow that logic at all. First, it seems to me a cynical admission that the statements which the Minister of Finance made in my presence in October and November, 1965, during the election campaign were not honest statements. I refer to the promise made by the Minister, and by other members of the government including the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), that these laws would all be passed and implemented immediately. If one sees

around Canada today, as every member of this house sees, a great deal of dissatisfaction among our people with the performance of this great institution; if one finds a great deal of cynicism and apathy among the people of Canada, I suggest with all the force I can that one of the reasons-not the only reason-is the callous way in which promises made at election time are disregarded, ignored and betrayed in action. Nothing can do this institution greater harm than the sequence which has occurred in the case of this law. Let us consider what has happened.
First, we had an election in November, 1965, in which the most solemn promise was made that there would be $105 per month minimum income provided for elderly people and that a medicare plan would be introduced immediately. In dealing with medicare, many of us have had the problem of declining in our own minds on the voluntary versus compulsory aspects of the scheme. I settled this issue in my mind with the thought that we were putting contributions from all the taxpayers of Canada toward a plan to ensure that every Canadian had at least minimum health services upon which they could rely. This, to my mind, made the compulsory aspect of the scheme attractive. I could solve the problem in my own conscience because nobody would be denied the benefits of good medical services on the ground that they could not afford them.
The argument that is being advanced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), with the Minister of National Health and Welfare as the unwitting Charley McCarthy bouncing up and down on his knee and saying what he is told to say, is that medicare has to be postponed for a year because it is inflationary. What crueller jest was ever perpetrated on the poor people of Canada, some of whom for 50 years have looked to this parliament to do something about their health needs.
For most Canadians, including the members of this chamber, there is no problem of inflation involved in health services. We either pay directly to medical doctors or we pay through group insurance plans. Either way, the payment is made and we receive health services
Medicare
in return for that payment. Under a medicare plan, if we adopt some different method of payment, in this case by payment of taxes, it would be a substitute payment for that which we have been making previously. How can anybody say that this is inflationary?
Approximately the same amount of dollars would be involved. They just go through a different economic channel than before. No flood of new money is created through this method of making payment for medical services. What might be considered inflationary by the Minister of Finance-although I really do not see how he can justify it in his conscience, or how anybody in this house could be allowed to justify it in their conscience-is that somehow we would be extending medical services to poor people who could not otherwise afford them and that this, in effect, constitutes inflation. Mr. Speaker, surely if we have one obligation as members of parliament, no matter to which party we belong, it is to provide the protection and help that society can give to people who cannot get that protection and help themselves. There have been great careers in the House of Commons dedicated to that proposition. Nobody, for example, will take from the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) his concern for the poor and helpless of this country.

My colleague from Skeena suggests that this might do it a lot of good. This might be a debatable point in some people's minds, but like the hon. member for Skeena I can assure the house that I am a very proud and loyal resident of the province of British Columbia. Indeed, I feel it does have much to offer for the emulation of the rest of Canada. If I may say so, I do not refer in this connection to the kind of government administration we have there at this particular moment in time.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, I think it has become obvious from some of the discussions which have taken place in connection with incorporations, reincorporations or ex-tentions of insurance companies which have been placed before us that some of us are much concerned over what has become a very evident trend in Canada at the present time. As my colleague from Timiskaming suggests, we are beginning to wonder, if the charters of all these new insurance companies were stretched end to end, whether we would have a paper sidewalk extending from one end of Canada to the other. However, we have indicated that our concern over what is happening in the whole field of investment of funds in Canada is deep and real.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
We regard this rash of bills designed to expand and multiply the operations of private insurance companies as being a reprehensible step. Some hon. members have suggested that this is a right under what we call a free enterprise economy. We have tried to explain that while we have some recognition of the value of competition in productive enterprises, our view is that insurance companies as they have operated in the past and as they are operating now, are not really competitive and are certainly not productive of new wealth in this country. We believe their effect is to deflect the savings of Canadian citizens in certain directions, and our position, as is well known, is that it would be more desirable if the savings of our people were channelled in directions which would ensure that the flow of investments would be in a correct proportion according to the needs of the economy and the Canadian people as a whole.
The net effect of the proliferation of these companies is to reduce the flow of investment funds available in Canada at a time when we are in dire need of investment capital. We believe the multiplicity of overhead charges involved in the kind of expansion of which this

bill is an example simply reduces the residual amount which is available for capital development in this country in any direction, leaving aside the question of whether or not a greater proportion of available savings should be directed in such a manner as to come under public control. It seems to me that these repeated proposals for the incorporation of life insurance companies should cause us particular concern in the light of certain of the discussions which have taken place in this chamber in recent weeks, and of statements of the kind made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) about the inflationary pressures on the economy.
There has been a good deal of talk about tight money. I am suggesting that if we continue to permit the multiplication of insurance companies which will siphon off more and more of the savings of the Canadian people, the fears expressed by the Minister of Finance and others about what some people call "tight money" will become increasingly well founded. I draw the attention of the house to the superfluous overhead expenses brought about by a multiplicity of office operations which shift more and more Canadians into what I deem to be useless and unproductive occupations.
So it is with regret and concern that I see these bills being introduced one after another, particularly when in this instance, as in others, the sponsor, the hon. member who accepts responsibility for introducing these measures into the chamber, has completely failed to justify his action in the terms set out in the preamble to the bill where it is stated: it is expedient to enact this legislation. My basic argument is that it is not expedient to do so and for this reason, as far as I am concerned, this proposal, together with similar proposals, should be rejected by the house.
My contention is that the house should turn its attention to much more fruitful ways of ensuring that we enjoy an expanding economy in which the net savings of the Canadian people can be devoted to useful and constructive purposes.

Mr. Speaker, before private members' hour I was attempting to explain to the house the reason the government had sought this particular way to deal with the problem of the old age pensioner by providing for a guaranteed income program as the most effective way to give maximum support to old age pensioners on low or modest incomes. I contrasted this approach to the approach put forward by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) namely, a straight increase of $25 per month in the flat rate pension. Possibly the impact of this particular proposal was not clearly understood at the resolution stage, but the fact is that the alternative scheme put forward by the Leader of the Opposition would represent $60 less in income support per year for the more than
500.000	recipients of old age security in Canada today who have no income other than their old age security pension. The effect of the alternative proposal, in comparison to the government proposal, would take away at least $30 million from those on low or modest incomes and redistribute that amount of money among the higher income groups.
I illustrated the effect of this proposition by one example which was used merely to show the difference in the approach espoused by the government and that espoused by the Leader of the Opposition. We believe that by not providing income support over the whole range of the spectrum of incomes received by recipients of old age security we are able to do more for those on low and modest incomes.

I should like to go on to say that in my view the government has responsibll.ties toward all sections of the Canadian population. It is not always easy to balance these respons.bilit.es jud.ciously. Clearly, we owe it to our older people, who have borne the burdens of the past half century, to ensure that they have a decent and adequate income for their retirement years. But we also have an obligation not to impose undue or avoidable taxation on those who are now earning and who are trying to provide for themselves and their families.
In our view the guaranteed income approach is the best and fairest way of balancing these obligations. It will provide maximum help to those on low and modest incomes while keeping tax increases or the tax burden to a minimum.
I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has made the point, and is likely itching to make it again, that there is a current surplus in the old age security fund. As hon. members know, additional funds will be required to finance the guaranteed income program. There is only one source for these additional funds, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has already indicated his intention to introduce a budget at least in part for this purpose. An increase in taxes is never a pleasant occurrence, but I suggest such unpleasantness would be considerably more extensive if the opposition proposal were put into effect.
I am sure the people of this country want to see a decent and adequate retirement income for our older people and are prepared to accept a redistribution of income for this purpose. I am also sure that they expect the federal government to effect this redistribution in a way which will make maximum use of the nation's financial resources at this stage of our development and in view of present demands upon our economy and resources. This the guaranteed income formula does. It will place those on low or modest incomes above the $100 a month standard proposed by the official opposition without diverting revenue into some pockets which are already prosperous pockets.
A comparison of the cost of the guaranteed income program and the $25 a month increase shows the validity of this argument. Current estimates are that the income supplement will cost between $260 million and $280 million in its first year. This is approximately $100 million less than the cost of a $25 a month increase in the flat rate pension. The cost of a flat rate increase would go up each year so that by 1970 the extra burden on the federal treasury would be something in the neighbourhood of $200 million a year more than the cost of the guaranteed income supplement. At the expense of being repetitive I should like to reiterate that the benefits of this program will do more for pensioners who need it most at less cost to the Canadian taxpayer than the scheme advanced by the opposition parties. On the other hand, if I am not willing, if I am not strong enough, if I do not have this incentive to work, to make it short, if I stay home by the fire, the same government will give me $105; and this is what we call encouraging one to do one's best. It is in this sense that we consider that the bill is a step backward.
So much for the principles; let us now consider the facts. We will soon discover the unprecedented chaos which the government is asking us to accept-and enthusiastically, at that.
First, although the money which will be necessary in order to bring pensions up to modern requirements could be collected without a new law by means of a simple increase in taxes, which every citizen would understand, the enactment of the legislation brings about the creation of a completely new collecting system: new investigation department, new staff, new investigators and supervisors, new legal procedures, stationery, forms, offices, all completely unnecessary administration costs which could amount to thousands of dollars, if the principle is wrong from the beginning, if the law is unnecessary.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), in his speech at the resolution stage, placed that under the new approach heading. I would venture to say that this new approach is one of division, discrimination and discontent, which does not even have the merit of being new, since the government is unceasingly applying it.
As a second fact, the minister did not mention that, from now on, all old people, men and women, must fill out income tax returns,

Delays in the payments which those errors will involve, penalties, the necessity to resort to arbitration, representations, travelling inconveniences, claims for overpayments-because there will be some-year-end adjustments, waiting for retroactivity, uncertainty concerning real income, those are the many difficulties anticipated which will complicate their lives and make them dependent, as the minister said, on friends, neighbours, relatives and on civil employees. And this in the cases where only the minimum guarantee can be applied.
What about the unfortunate ones who will perhaps have the heart to work ten months a year and would deserve this basic $120? Because of this additional income they will have to fill out forms twice as complex, and the delays and personal difficulties will be multiplied by as much.
Third, a postponement of at least three months was announced at the very outset. Old Age Security Act Amendment calculated, before the fair and actual income was calculated. This will be submitting our elderly citizens to the jungle of bureaucracy.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, how many of our elderly citizens will have to resort to this famous appeal court mentioned by the minister. How many of our senior citizens will have to drag themselves before this court, perhaps for the first time in their lives, for the only crime of having grown old and contributed for years to the development of their country, and to be condemned, as a reward, to the jungle of bureaucracy which I just mentioned. I think those are the real difficulties which will complicate the lives of these people.
Fifth, the minister said to us in all confidence and frankness that the income from the sale of a property would not count for the minimum pension. I think he was speaking of the existing situation. But I also think that the situation will become so complicated, as it already is, that many of our pensioners who got their houses through hardship and effort, will have to sell them, because they will be too expensive to run. The minister tells us that there is absolutely no danger of that, that the proceeds from the sale of a house-which are already meagre enough as such-will not be considered as income in the determination of pension supplements. I am quite prepared to accept that assurance until the day when a government, any government, will levy a tax on, let us say, capital gains, which will then be considered as income.
I think that the minister will admit that what he is referring to are conditions which exist at the present time. But, as far as future conditions and new taxes are concerned, I do not think that he can predict that any more than I can. In other words, can he assure us that, in fact, capital gains will never be taken into account.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, as I said at the outset of my remarks, the alternative suggested by the opposition does not give rise to any of the objections in principle or in fact, which have been mentioned. It is but a simple rule to extend the application of a single principle already studied and accepted, already tested, to provide a guaranteed income of $100 or $105 a month, to which nobody would object.
Why, then, this innovation, this step into the unknown, this experiment whose exact cost, even, is unknown? I do not think my arguments on this subject can be refuted.

The other day I heard one of the hon. members opposite say that he had canvassed the elderly people in his riding with regard to this new plan, and that all approved of it. I think this is being naive. It means absolutely nothing except that these poor people are hungry, needy, and will accept anything at any price, even at the price of hardship, humiliation, freedom and peace of mind, for the simple reason that they are in need.
On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the hon. members will be ashamed to explain the chaos into which this legislation and this government are leading us. This legislation can only multiply the problems and increase the misery of those who deserve a better fate. The Minister of National Health and Welfare a couple of times read one of the recommendations from the report of the joint committee on the Canada Pension Plan, the one which called upon the government to do something about people who would not be drawing from the Canada Pension plan because of age. That recommendation can be found on page 1039 of Volume CXI, 1964-65, Journals of the House of Commons. But on page 1038 of the same volume there appears another recommendation made to this house
by the joint committee which reads as follows:
The level of combined benefits available under the Canada Pension Plan and old age security should represent a high proportion of the previous earnings of those people whose income does not permit other adequate provision for their retirement.
Le us look squarely at the situation. The whole justification for the Canada Pension Plan-and nobody supported it more strongly than I did and still do-was that by a combination of a flat rate pension under old age security and an earnings related program under the Canada Pension Plan, we could produce a total pension benefit that would be adequate for the people of this country. I remind the house that the amount a person can get under the Canada Pension Plan is only 25 per cent of his income up to the $5,000 ceiling. I am quite confident that when 1975 arrives the $5,000 income ceiling will have gone up and that the amount people can get under the Canada Pension Plan will also have gone up from the present $104 a month to a higher figure. If, when that figure goes up, you freeze the flat rate at $75, not only do you throw these two things out of balance, you produce the result that the total pension Canadians can receive will be a lower percentage of their incomes than is the case now.
The minister should not sit over there and laugh about this thing because it is very serious. He is changing the concept which was presented to this country when the Canada Pension Plan was brought into being. The minister suggests that we should not be political. I am prepared to be so far from political that he might not recognize what I mean when I say the Canada Pension Plan was a good proposition. I supported it and I still support it, but unless you match it with a flat rate pension that is also capable of increasing according to the increase in productivity you are destroying the whole basis of this joint plan which was put together a couple of years ago.
The admission by the minister that his so-called 40 per cent increase is transitional and temporary, and will start to fade out completely by 1975, is an admission that he is not increasing the flat rate of the old age pension, and this is wrong for the reasons I have indicated.
In th;s same connection I should like to sav, in terms that hon. members might regard as a l.ttle more simple, the th.ngs that are being said to me in the letters I receive every day in my mail. Elderly people are wondering why it is that increases in incomes seem to be possible for everybody else-as my correspondents put it, for workers and all kinds of people in various walks of life-but there can be no increase for old age pensioners. The point they make is well taken. If there has been an increase in productivity, an increase in affluence and an increase in our standard of living it is all right for workers and others to share in that increase, but so should the

The minister is throwing this joint package out of gear. Instead of reaching the point where people can get 60 per cent or 70 per cent of their lifetime earnings as a pension we are moving to a position where it will drop to 40 per cent or 45 per cent. As one element goes up the other goes down.
Let me suggest to the minister that our belief in a basic, genuine and honest increase in the flat amount of old age security pensions is not just a political belief for the moment; it is a bel'ef in a plan that will really stand up over the years.
When we were considering the resolution I pointed out that there were a number of points in connection with the scheme brought forward by the minister which produced elements of unfairness and discrimination. The minister likes to make the point that there is no means test applied as means tests have been described. He also likes to make the point that this whole thing is very s:mple. I have read the bill but I do not th;nk it is quite as simple as he suggests. Let me repeat the question I put to him when he was making h s speech this evening. For the last 15 or 16 years people have had a sense of pride in being on the old age pension. It was something one could boast about and say, "I am a pensioner",

because it carried no suggestion that there was any poverty involved or that one had to go through any kind of test to get it. But from now on, if one says he is a pensioner the question will be asked, what kind of pensioner is he? Is he one who gets only $75 because he is a senator or has other revenue and does not need the supplement, or does he get the supplement because he is poor and has gone through this business of reporting his income on a simple income tax form which the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) has worked out?
I see the minister nodding his head. We will see how simple that form and the process are when the time comes. As I pointed out the other day, if it is so simple it is strange that it will take to the end of March before any payments are made and to the end of April before some are made. All this delay could be avoided by a simple increase to $105 a month. It does not take much to change the machines that print these cheques; they could easily be changed to print the cheques to read $105 a month instead of $75.
Mr. Speaker, at times I am diverted by my hon. friends across the chamber. The point I was trying to make was that when you have to report your income you immediately get into a situation where different pensioners with about the same amount of income will find that in one case one will get the supplement and another will not. Let us take the case of war disability pensioners. They do not pay income tax on their war disability pension. Therefore I take it they will not get the supplement. But the war veterans allowance recipient, even though he does not pay income tax on his war veterans allowance, and even though the minister says he will give that person the supplement, is under a means test as far as the War Veterans Allowance Act is concerned. So what you give him with one hand is taken away with the other.
You will have the same problem with the provincial supplements. The minister stands up in all his Scroogian generosity and says provincial supplements will not be counted; people can still get this supplement even though they are getting the provincial supplement. The minister had his little fun, of course, reminding me that I like to refer to the surplus in the old age security fund. I do not mind him putting it that way, although that is not the way I have been describing it for the past number of months. We were telling the government last June and July about this unused surplus in the fund, so in the summer the government moved some of that money out of the fund into the consolidated revenue fund. I recognize that is legal. I am not suggesting this is a

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in
December 8, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment this great and fine discussion about the increase in old age pensions.
I find, Mr. Speaker, that we are now discussing and complicating the financial situation of the aged. The situation is getting more .complex as we go along. Our older people bave a right to expect something better than the shabby policy we are advocating and the pettiness we are showing in an attempt to Improve this legislation.
I say to the minister that this legislation is merely red tape and that the more we move forward in an economy which should be sound and free while providing for a decent living, the more we are mistaken and the more we complicate matters.
Mr. Speaker, this improvement to the Old Age Security Act is so complicated that it is hardly understandable.
The hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Regimbal) explained the situation quite well. He went into all the details of that set-up; as it is now, I think that we would be better off without any at all. Why act like a Scrooge when it comes to allocate the country's production in a country which is bursting with wealth?
Mr. Speaker, do the old people clothe themselves with dollar bills? Do they use dollars for food? Is it dollars that they will use for medicine and for fuel? It is the production of the country which they need, on their table and in their closets, and that production exists and is easy to allocate. But, instead of feeling compassion for their fate and admitting that our country produces abundantly, we feel compassion for the fate of money. We want our old people to partake of this abundance on the basis of the money available and if we do not find the required amounts through taxes and taxation increases, we are very cautious not to specify that an increase in pensions, will automatically trigger an increase in all kinds of taxes, so that the [DOT]old people may avail themselves of the commodities already produced.
The minister knows fully well that in 1966 our production was worth $56 billion and that only $38 billion were distributed. He should .also know that there is enough left for our old people to live decently and that this [DOT]distribution must take place.
Money, sir, is only a symbol. It is but an instrument of barter to obtain commodities, to produce, to fulfill needs. And if, in fact, production does not fulfill the needs, then the *economy is in a state of turmoil.


Instead of reforming the economy, they talk about reforming our older people. They talk about establishing a system and having the aged adjust to the new system. Any system must be developed to be used. Everything which exists is meant to be used. And all those instruments serve no purpose; so if they do not help fulfill the needs, then it is useless to try and distribute anything or do anything better.
Strangely enough, money can never be found to enable the people to live decently, when it would be so easy to do. Yet, all organizations or institutions are allowed to increase their interest rates, for instance. Large institutions are allowed to make more and more profits, to build up reserves and to conceal them and the minister is even forbidden to interfere in that respect. The minister is prevented from meddling with those reserves which are not declared for income tax purposes, without any regard for the economy.
Well, Mr. Speaker, our economy is quite unbalanced. And instead of trying to stabilize it and give it new impetus, it is being thrown still more out of balance.
Mr. Speaker, such stinginess is unwarranted. It is wrong to be stingy when it comes to our old people and the means to give them what they need. The way the minister has presented his bill, and the improvements he wants to make, none of that suits the taxpayers, or the old people.
Subject old people to regulations, income tax inspectors and all kinds of investigations, well, Mr. Speaker, I must tell the minister that it would shorten the life of all the old people. What we want in this country is freedom. And we can give a minimum of freedom to Canadians, to our old people as long as it does not interfere with the freedom of others.
And I feel that old people should be granted that pension without any restriction; it should be given directly, without restriction, without inspection and without any automatic control by the bureaucracy. That red tape, Mr. Speaker, grieves our citizens. Canadians pay dearly for it. The red tape to be inflicted upon the aged will cost more than the supplementary pension you want to give them.
Therefore, I ask the minister to reconsider his policy. We are not opposed to increased pensions to the aged. We are in favour, because we know that by giving them more money there will be more purchasing power in Canada. And that is what we need. If

CANADIAN ECONOMY-IMPOSITION OF CEILING ON FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you and the hon. members of this house for giving me an opportunity to explain the question I put, on Thursday afternoon, December 1, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters). For the benefit of the minister and of hon. members, the question was as follows:
Has he considered the possibility of imposing a ceiling on food prices in 1967?
The reasons which urged me to put this question to this government are many; I shall limit myself to listing a few.
There is serious concern among the Canadian people on the eve of Expo, as evidenced by this press report, from Le Soleil of last November 29:
The Canadian Restaurant Owners Association will present a brief to the federal government on or about December 10 asking for the establishment of a board to place a ceiling on food prices in 1967, such as the government imposed during the war. According to Mr. Cova, the co-ordinator of the association for the province of Quebec, the price of food is fixed according to the stockmarket demand, "which is ridiculous".
The request of this group has been made because, according to Mr. Cova, the federal government took no steps to reassure the population when a fantastic increase in the price of meat was announced for the following year. In this respect, the coordinator said that he thought the price of meat would not double, much less increase threefold.
The Canadian Restaurant Owners Association, whose chairman for metropolitan Quebec is Mr. George Tcharos, noted the present scarcity of foodstuffs which will last until Expo 67. The wholesalers, said the restaurant owners, are stocking their warehouses with foodstuffs which they will release only in the spring, when there will be a very great demand.
Already foods such as green peas and turkeys are becoming scarce, because they lie in warehouses. According to Mr. Roger Dulude, all the Montreal warehouses are full.
Mr. Speaker, there have always been profiteers, speculators, people who have no scruples in making exorbitant profits particularly on occasions such as the one we are getting ready to celebrate in 1967.
10912	COMMONS

It would be utopic to request from the established authority absolute control of these insatiable leeches; I think it is the duty of the government to take the necessary steps to protect the population from the tentacles of these vampires brought forth by the big financial enterprises.
Moreover, we are told with emphasis that the Canadian income from the tourist industry will reach $1 billion next year and that this is expected to double in the next decade. In fact, I think it is plausible to endorse these expectations, because our country will be invaded by a host of visitors who will attend the Expo and take this opportunity to visit our country from coast to coast. In my opinion, exploiting the tourists would be giving them a very bad reception.
On November 28 last, the federal-provincial conference on tourism opened in Ottawa. The purpose of that meeting was to find out how tourism could remain an economic enterprise after the centennial in 1967. Provincial, federal and regional representatives attended the three-day meeting and reviewed the main problems now facing the tourist industry.
In the light of the reasons I just mentioned,
I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) what policy he intends to follow to check the abuses which are always possible and which could prove prejudicial to the future of the Canadian nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter which I should like to discuss this evening relates to the grounds of parliament hill and substantial permanent alterations to those grounds without the knowledge of, or opportunity for discussion by parliament. It arises out of my attempt yesterday to obtain assurance from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith), who is the responsible minister in respect of this matter, that in future no such substantial alterations will be made affecting parliament hill by way of alterations in ingress or egress or by way of erection of permanent structures without the kind of notice which will give parliament the opportunity to discuss them. Unfortunately, yesterday I was unable to obtain that assurance, although I would have thought that any government which did not arrogate to itself the function of ownership of the grounds of parliament would give that assurance very readily.
If you will refer sir, to page 10811 of Hansard you will find the issue fully set out. I only emphasize once again that 1 am talking about permanent alterations and not the pinpricking type of alterations to which the minister referred such as changes in the windows of the parliament buildings or the putting up of some flags around the front entrance. My question makes perfectly clear that that is not the type of thing with which I was dealing.
23033-690J
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion What was asked by way of assurance from the government was recognition of the fact that the buildings and grounds of parliament hill are the property of the people of Canada and not the perquisite of the Liberal government or any other government of the day. They are not a great preserve of one government, as seemed to be indicated by the attitude taken by the minister yesterday.
This matter is not important just because of a difference between myself and the minister or the fact that I am a Conservative and the minister is a Liberal minister. Unfortunately in the past we have seen some illustrations of very real dangers in this regard. I think particularly of the situation concerning the west block when one of the minister's predecessors, who was a member of the party to which the present minister belongs, proposed that that building be demolished. That was before 1957.
At that time we took the position that it should not be demolished, that it was one of the most historic buildings in Canada and that the whole of the parliament buildings are part of the history of Canada. Fortunately we were able to carry our point. We were able to do so only because we had notice of the government's intention. It was a substantial project and therefore notice had to be given by way of an item in the government's estimates. The matter came up in the house and we were able to block the intention of the then minister. Therefore the west block was preserved and the inside of that historic building was remodelled. When we came into office we had the honour and privilege of carrying that project into effect, with the result that one can see now that all the historic and traditional aspects of the west block have been preserved and that it is a useful and valuable part of the whole complex of the parliament buildings and the site of parliament.
I have mentioned this example, sir, because I wanted to emphasize how fortunate it was that members of parliament representing the people of Canada had notice of the government's intention and were able to debate that intention. speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-255, to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code (Square Deal).

maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE TIME LIMIT ON APPLICATION RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE TIME LIMIT ON APPLICATION RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canada Labour (Standards) Code in part I sets hours of work at eight in a day and 40 in a week for businesses operating under federal jurisdiction. There is another provision in the act which permits the deferment or suspension of the application of those hours of work not exceeding 18 months after an application is made by any person so to defer or suspend them. Another section of the act, section 53, provides for an automatic suspension upon application.
The working together of sections 51 and 53 of the act could mean the perpetual deferment of the application of the hours of work section in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. In fact, this month is 18 months from the coming into force of the act and there are still a number of outstanding applications and consequent deferments of the application of the law.
My bill seeks to set certain time limits beyond which the deferment or suspension of the application of part I will not apply; in other words, to set a time limit beyond which they will not go. A square deal, therefore, Mr. Speaker, is a thing with which we plug a loophole.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

The old age pension is one way of doing it, of circulating more money, for the good of our economy, while helping each and every citizen who should have enough purchasing power to meet his material, intellectual and spiritual needs according to his nature and his daily, monthly and annual requirements.
Our government, the highest authority, the highest institution in this country is responsible for the welfare of each citizen, and not only for the prosperity of its great production, finance and business institutions. Why is it, sir, that all our big institutions are so prosperous as compared with human beings, several of whom five in hardship, destitution, insecurity, particularly when they reach old age, the age for rest, the age for retirement?

In years past, Mr. Speaker, all our old farmers had their own farms, their own cars, their own implements, their own livestock and their own production; they passed them on to their sons, who could marry while they were young without having to rely on the government for a living at any period of their lives.
Now, Mr. Speaker, why do old age pensions, and this can be said of all sectors of the economy, have to be increased, reorganized and readjusted? Salaries have to be raised, prices go up, people go on strike and request salary increases. The economy has never been in such a mess. The economy can no longer regain its equilibrium; it is constantly out of balance. And among those who are delegated to administer the country, to keep the economy in balance, nobody seems to be able to strike and maintain a proper balance between goods and distribution of goods, so as to permit each individual to live decently, as he has the right to expect, in a country where science, progress and development in every field have been accepted, in short, in a country where scientific progress outshines even the imagination of many citizens.
In 1966, in this 20th century of science and development, everybody in Canada should have a guarantee of solvent and adequate security. But we do not have it yet. We are still discussing ways and means to fight poverty. Poverty is everywhere. However, we apply the wrong methods to settle the problem. As a matter of fact, we pass legislation and regulations impoverishing the great majority of our citizens.
How come, Mr. Speaker, that governments nowadays have to hand every individual money to provide, from the cradle to the grave, for his basic needs and essentials of life. What is the cause of this general uneasiness?
It is said and repeated again and again that goods are plentiful in all parts of the country; the only shortage is in the purchasing power of people. The source of this uneasiness, Mr. Speaker, lies nowhere else. Let each senior citizen have the necessities of life, the daily essentials, without investigation, as a matter of right as a citizen, in the name of personal dignity, by his right as a full member of the Canadian nation, and you will see a change in all this atmosphere of want, poverty, misery or concern, which stifles the joy of living in all Canadian homes, in this wage-earning class, the farmers of today.

Mr. Speaker, in beginning my remarks this afternoon I should like to congratulate the minister upon his vision in bringing in legislation providing for a guaranteed annual income. I recall that some months ago in this house I urged him strongly to do this, and it pleases me that he has. I regret in a way that he has set the figures for the proposed guaranteed annual income so low and on such a fine borderline that the advantage of it cannot be clearly seen by many of the people who will be affected by this measure.
I trust the minister will be amenable to accepting amendments that will raise the figures to a point where the tremendous advantages of this plan will become more obvious than they are at the present time, when the advantages are clouded by the paucity of the figures presented to us. While I congratulate the minister on his vision, I must take some time to say that this idea is not new in the world and is certainly not new to Canada. Many, many years ago Social Credit began urging on the governments of this country that income be provided to its citizens more directly than has been the case up to the present time.
Old Age Security A.ct Amendment
I recall that when the Social Credit movement began in Canada its founder, Major Douglas, frequently said that political action by Social Crediters would not be necessary if governments did what they should in the line of legislation. Usually, and the pattern has been repeated over and over again, governments have been so intransigent that people who have believed in Social Credit principles have had to be involved in political action in order to allow for change at all. But when change comes, as it is coming now, and is coming from whatever party happens to be in power in this country, I feel we should welcome it because of the line that has been proudly developed by Social Credit in this country for many years.
The concept of the guaranteed annual income has been explored considerably. One of the people who has had a great deal to say about it is the economist Robert Theobald. In his book "The Guaranteed Income" he makes a very fine argument for applying the guaranteed annual income to the aged. I should like to quote from that argument at the beginning of my remarks. He says:
There should be no need to justify payments to the physically and mentally ill: they cannot work and society should surely provide for them.
He goes on to say:
Some justification, however, is often felt to be required for more adequate payments to the old, for one of the most sanctified of our work myths is that older people both could and should have saved enough to provide for their old age. This is, of course, merely a cynical fiction. Those who are old today worked in an era when their income was necessarily far lower than is paid for jobs demanding a comparable level of skills and application today. They needed to spend a large proportion of their income just to cover their expenses, including the education of their children. They were therefore able to save very little, if anything, whether directly or through insurance schemes. Today's labour force, however, would not be enjoying its present level of income without their hard work and that of earlier generations who had even less to show for their toil. Any fair distribution of the nation's resources should ensure that old people be allowed to share in the wealth they created. Their labour was, in fact, wealth, and it was invested in the national economy at a time when its value was at a premium. Today this group should be collecting their "earned interest."
I think this is the soundest justification for the guaranteed annual income for the aged. The book also holds out a hope that eventually a proper application of this plan will be made and we might look forward to some of the things to which Keynes the economist was referring when he said:
When the accumulation of wealth is no longer of high social importance, there will be great

changes in the code ol morals. We shall be able to rid ourselves of many of the pseudo-moral principles which have hag-ridden us for two hundred years, by which we have exalted some of the most distasteful of human qualities into the position of the highest values. We shall be able to afford to dare to assess the money-motive at its true value... All kinds of social customs and economic practices affecting the distribution of wealth and its rewards and penalties which we now maintain at all costs, however distasteful and unjust they may be in themselves... we shall then be free, at last, to discard.

I could not help thinking, as I listened to the hon. member then that that great prairie figure, the late William Aberhart, must have looked down and smiled to himself as he heard the words of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The hon. member said:

If this is to be accepted as a principle, then I suggest it be accepted more than as a matter of words.
The hon. member then used these terribly important words:
Our legislation should be based on it.

Of course one of them is that when he looked at the guaranteed annual income at that time he saw it as a levelling process which would bring every citizen to exactly the same point on the economic scale. Those who are pessimistic about the nature of man and who therefore oppose a guaranteed income will be joined by those who prefer to maintain present organizational patterns in the face of changing technology, for this will allow them to control their subordinates or employees and, indeed, the population as a whole through the job mechanism.
Certainly this fear of automation has given the New Democratic Party a tremendous lever of control.
Another effect of the guaranteed annual income concept is the fact that it strikes at the whole concept of the elite in the welfare state, and I mentioned this in previous speeches in the house. The idea did not originate with the
December 9, 1966

New Democratic Party; in tact it was picked up in passing by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and by one or two others, but it has since been dropped because it has been taken out of their hands by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and by the government in this legislation.
The final reason, I suspect, for the change of heart on the part of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is that the proper administration in this country of the guaranteed annual income will remove once and for all from the political arena the old age security pension, a move which has been long overdue.
I would hope that what we heard last night was one of the last gasps of those who have been happy throughout the years to use the old age security pension as a political football to kick around in whatever direction suited them best.
I have received representations from old age pensioners who have been fearful of the idea of the guaranteed annual income and who want to maintain the status quo, that is the present system of allotting old age pensions. The question I asked them, and which has not been answered to my satisfaction, was: How can you depend on a system which has always left old age security pensions so far behind in the economic scale in this country? I told them they had nothing to lose in the guaranteed annual income system, and a considerable amount to gain from it.
At this point I should like to give the minister some advice, because I know that many old age pensioners are extremely sceptical of the scheme. He has a tremendous task in front of him if he wishes to sell this scheme to pensioners across this country. The word "guaranteed" must mean that the government accepts the provision laid down in the old age security pension legislation, that the old age pension cannot be attached, as is done at present by various departments of the government to collect what they call overpayments which have been made to old age pensioners.
What the minister can do is to grant a reprieve to those old age pensioners who have been forced to return the overpayments which have been made to them through no fault of their own. One case at least has been brought to my attention, and the department involved has acknowledged its responsibility for the mistake. Overpayments to the value of $400 have been paid out, and collected unwittingly by the recipient, who subsequently was presented with a bill for that amount. The

Old Age Security Act Amendment process of repayment has been going on at the rate of $10 a month for some time now, and will continue in the future; so that the old age security pension of this man has not amounted to $75 for the last year, but is only $65 as he continues to pay off the sum of money which he collected through no fault of his.
I know I am not alone in presenting such cases. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has raised this matter before in the house and argued well on it. I cannot think of any one move which would make the old age pensioners of this country more confident that the government has their best interests at heart, and is actually going to guarantee the old age security pension, than an announcement by the minister that these bills will be written off as an uncollectable debt, once the legislation is passed.
It will encourage these people to know that when the minister says the guaranteed annual income will insure that the income of the old age pensioners of this country will not fall below $105, he means exactly this. When old age pensioners fill out the form, regardless of how simple it is, they will have doubts that somehow they have not done the right thing and they have missed something. This will be a haunting fear to them because they know of the experiences of others, and they will be afraid they will eventually be presented with a bill for overpayments because of some mistake. Dickens' Scrooge had very little resemblance to the man who, in the very short period of time that the present minister has held his portfolio, has brought in three comprehensive pieces of legislation-the Canada Assistance Plan, the medicare plan, and now these amendments to the Old Age Security Act. I think this is a tremendous record and it will be a long time before any minister in the future will duplicate it.
My motivation for participating in this debate was not, of course, to extol the virtues of

the minister-I think his talents are recognized in all parts of the house-but basically to answer a challenge offered by the premier of the province of Quebec, who suggested that members of parliament from Quebec participate in this debate and express their opinions, preferably of course to bolster the arguments of the premier that the federal government has no place in this particular field of legislation.
