My opening comments are important because in speaking on this bill and referring to the arguments advanced by the premier of Quebec, I wish it to be understood that if I differ from him, it is strictly on academic grounds.
I do not pretend to the house, or to Mr. Johnson, to be another expert on the constitution of Canada. My knowledge of the constitution is no greater or less than that of other members of the house. I have said before, and I repeat now, that I am not a lawyer. Like Mr. Johnson, I hope I am a realist; and when I interpret the constitution, when I interpret any constitution, whether it is the constitution of Canada, or that of the local Kiwanis or Lions Club, I tend to interpret it in the light of the end result the constitution was designed to achieve.
In the final analysis, when the Fathers of Confederation agreed to include all the provinces of this country in confederation under the British North America Act, they wanted what was best for the country. They wanted
10932	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment what was best for Quebec, for Ontario or for any other province of this country. For this reason I am a little puzzled by the desire of Quebec to assert itself now in the field of old age security pensions, particularly as the federal government has provided pensions to our senior citizens legally since 1952.
Most constitutional experts support the view that section 94(a) of the British North America Act does not deny the right of the provinces to provide old age security pensions. The section says, rather, that the federal government may do so also, at the same time as the provinces. Certainly I would not be thinking of the best interests of Quebec if I were to advocate that Quebec establish and finance its own plan at this late date and impose the necessary taxes to support, it. Certainly such a plan would put the senior citizens of Quebec in an enviable position, because they would receive federal and provincial benefits, but the double taxation load would be too heavy to carry. Certainly the money thus raised by new taxes could be put to better use by being directed, in my province, to the needs of education.
Speaking as a pragmatist and as one who on numerous occasions has stressed the right of the province in many areas, particularly in the field of education, I cannot understand how the aspirations of Quebec-the aim to close the financial gap between itself and other provinces; the problem of the survival of the French language; the right of French speaking Quebeckers to speak their own language at work; the right of French speaking Quebeckers to survive culturally in an ever growing mass of English speaking peoples on the North American continent-are to be helped by assuming responsibility in the field of old age security.
With all the problems existing in the province of Quebec, will the province's aspirations come closer to realization by transferring to it the responsibility and heavy financial burden of providing old age security pensions to its senior citizens? As a Quebecker I can think of the problem of poverty in urban areas, of the need to eliminate slums in the big cities, of the physical expansion necessary in the field of education.

Wheat Sale to Mainland China
I should like to point out one fact. The time has come for a substantial increase in the price of wheat. I do not know what the price is under this contract, but this government during its period in office cut the price of wheat 18 cents a bushel. In the last year and a half, this reduction has caused a loss of $150 million to western farmers. Now that the minister has been out west and has come out in favour of an increase in the wheat prices under the international wheat agreement, I hope that this government will be able not only to restore the 18 cents a bushel it cut off but also an additional amount.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the announcement which just has been made I am sure will be welcome news to all Canadians, but in particular to the wheat producers on the Canadian prairies. Leader of the Opposition.
We can continue to show an impressive record of wheat exports and yet still leave the western wheat producer in the unfortunate position that what he receives in return for his production is inadequate to ensure a healthy prairie economy. Mr. Speaker, I join the previous speakers in expressing our pleasure at the news that Canada has just concluded a new sale to China. This will surely be significant to the whole economy of Canada but will be of particular benefit to the western producers. I congratulate them, first
December 9, 1966

Wheat Sale to Mainland China of all, for setting up the Canadian Wheat Board which enables them to have markets scaled to their production and guarantees the sale of their production. We are proud for them. They surely cannot blame us, in the east, for trying to at least imitate them by requesting the establishment of a board to handle eastern produce.
I feel that if eastern Quebec had a body similar to the one created for the west, we could take pride in having accomplished some progress, instead of realizing, from year to year, what calamities befall our farmers for lack of markets for their farm produce. This year again, we have a typical example in the province of Quebec, and particularly in my area, where the farmers will lose 50 per cent of their produce because they are unable to sell them.
I congratulate the Canadian Wheat Board, as well as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) its principal agent, for, I believe, he is honorary president of the board. That alone is a big advantage. I feel they have all the advantages on their side. I do not envy them; I am proud of them. Incidentally, I ask the federal government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce to find some grounds, some good reason, to help the eastern farmers as much they do the western producers.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the wheat producers on the prairies of course have had a record breaking crop [DOT]during the growing season of 1966 and, therefore, any additional firm sales will be welcomed. This will move the wheat into world trade rather than have it build up into a surplus position on the farms, which we experienced through most of the 1950's.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Beer) three or four quesitons with regard to this sale, because I think it is becoming increasingly clear not only to Canadian producers but also to producers of grain all over the world that there will be far larger quantities of wheat going into international trade in the immediate future than we have experienced in the past. In other words, the levels which we thought were normal in so far as export trade is concerned have moved up substantially. I think this has placed producers in a little more favourable position in respect of prices, as those prices relate to the cost of production.
There has not been an appreciable increase in the price of wheat for a long time, although the costs have in fact gone up. I did not hear
[Mr. Gauthier.)
the hon. member clearly when he mentioned the period during which the wheat is to be delivered. However, since this now is a firm contract for 900,000 long tons, I presume, that a firm price has been affixed to the contract whether or not the delivery period in fact does extend beyond the termination of the present international wheat contract.
[DOT] (1:10 p.m.)
We agree with the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) that there is now a need for an upward revision of this maximum price. If there is a large part of this contract to be delivered at a firm price, notwithstanding any increase in the maximum price, this perhaps will not be advantageous to some producers.
So far as delivery is concerned, I hope that the Canadian Wheat Board and the Department of Transport have considered all the implications involved in moving this large amount of wheat to export positions, bearing in mind the other commitments which have been made. I certainly hope that a committee on transportation will take into account the enormous task involved in delivering this wheat to export positions.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary whether or not there is a firm part of this contract which will be delivered in the form of flour and, if not, whether negotiations were carried out by the Canadian Wheat Board to deliver some of this grain in the form of flour.
In closing let me say that we welcome this announcement and believe, as other speakers have indicated, that the time has finally arrived when there is a market condition favourable to increasing the price to the point at which it should be.

When we reach committee stage let us stop this petty wrangling between parties and for once unite in a common desire to do what is best for the senior citizens of this country. In the light of partisan politics and their blind fervour to emerge as the party in power or the official opposition, the N.D.P. is quite willing to use the emotions and affections of the senior citizens and treat them as callously as they did the farmers when the hon. member's party was known as the C.C.F. If there is anybody in the House of Commons who is using-and I use the word "using" in its worst sense-the affections of the senior citizens of this country, it is the socialists who run up and down the country claiming that they are the voice of the senior citizens in the House of Commons. But when there is an opportunity to support legislation and improve the circumstances of our senior citizens, legislation that is aimed at helping those who need help most by putting $38 million more into their pockets, these hon. members ask questions such as the question asked by the hon. member for Danforth. I believe that when the senior citizens of this country realize the implications and the imaginative aspects of this bill, and for the first time realize they are not being used as pawns in the chess game of politics, they will look upon the New Democratic Party, and rightly so, as a party of false propaganda.

Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult indeed to follow an address such as the one made by the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey). I do not know just how I should refer to his talk in the house today. It seemed to be two things: first, an exercise in governmental approbation and, second, a biographical discourse. Whatever it was in actual fact I can only say that it had very little to do with the bill before the house. The hon. member made a very scathing statement with reference to what he called "the egalitarian concept of universality". Of course he was referring to the proposal to increase old age pensions across the board to $100 a month. It was strange to hear this from the government benches. I did not hear the concept of universality in the medicare bill referred to as an egalitarian concept. I wonder precisely what the difference is. In all the speeches which have been made in this debate the one thing which seemed to be in doubt was the precise understanding of what a means test is. The minister has spoken twice; once on the resolution and again yesterday in second reading. He spent most of his time pointing out that the income test suggested in the bill, is not a means test at all.
As a matter of fact he went further than that. On page 10894 of Hansard he is reported as having said the following:
Anyone who equates the means test with the norms set out in this program is either stupid or dishonest.
In other parts of his speech he refers to the attempts to make political hay out of the discussion of the guaranteed income program. The minister said it is terrible to do such a thing. He is imputing motives to us which, I
December 9, 1966	COMMONS
would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, are neither tactual nor fair and certainly are beneath the dignity of the position which the minister holds. So far as I am concerned, I do not think there is a single member in the house who does not have the welfare of the senior citizens of our country at heart. I think the house is no place for such allegations, especially when they are made by a minister of the Crown. We may disagree as to the methods which we feel should be used to bring about a proper basic income for our senior citizens, but I do not think we should use this difference to impute such motives as the minister has suggested.
In his remarks the minister seems to have attempted to pre-empt the position of purity and sincerity which has been held previously by another group in the house. It seems to me that this is exactly what he was trying to do. On the one hand, he expressed a tremendous concern-and I certainly do not doubt his sincerity in this-for the welfare of the old age pensioners, and he said that he and his government are the only ones to express this concern. However, I would hazard a guess that the people of Canada will know where we on this side of the house stand. After listening to the various remarks of the minister, I wonder whether they will know where he really stands. The position of the gentlemen on the other side of the house seems to change with the political weather vanes. I do not think there are many old age pensioners in this country who have forgotten the "six buck boys" of 1957. If we wanted to refer to changing with political weather vanes, we would have to go back a lot further than that.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
We can go back, Mr. Speaker, to 1951 when the Old Age Security Bill was brought into this house by the government of the day. In this regard, I should like to refresh the memories of hon. gentlemen opposite, though I fully realize that the present minister was not in the house at that time.
I should like to refer to page 1 of Hansard for October 9, 1951 and read a few lines from the speech from the throne of that day:
The primary reason for summoning you for a second session in the present year is to invite your consideration of a measure to provide increased security for our older citizens through payment of pensions, without a means test and as a matter of right-
In 1951 the present minister of external affairs occupied the portfolio which is now occupied by the minister of health and welfare, and he spoke most eloquently, as is his
Old Age Security Act Amendment wont, on this subject of old age security payments without a means test. He emphasized this in his speech many times. Although I do not think there is anything to be gained by reading his whole speech into the record, certainly a few of the remarks he made are very appropriate at this time.
I might mention in passing that I have read the speeches of some other hon. gentlemen who were members of the house in 1951, and I must say that the speech the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) delivered yesterday was exactly the same as the speech he made then. The only change was the figures.
I think the one thing that will become clear is that, whereas the position of the government has been changing with the political weather vanes, the position of members on this side of the house has not changed during these many years. The minister tosses his head and does not believe this; let me convince him.
As reported at page 380 of Hansard for October 25, 1951, the then minister of health and welfare had this to day:
The legislative proposals which will be brought forward following approval of this resolution are, in essence, the same proposals on old age security which the federal government advanced at that time.
He is referring to 1945.
The concept of a universal old age pension-
There is no mention here of the egalitarian concept.
-free of means test, which was first advanced in 1945, was then regarded as bold and original. Many persons, some governments included, were not yet ready to accept a proposal which broke so sharply with the traditional means test approach of the past.
At that time, family allowances,-
They are still in effect today.
-the first and hitherto the greatest of these new programs, based on similar principles, had not yet been fully accepted by all political parties, nor even by all sections of the general public.
There were those who said that the government, in its thinking on social questions, was getting too far ahead of the thinking of the people:-
It may have been then, but believe me, Mr. Speaker, the government are miles behind today.
-that the people were not ready for these new and sweeping universal programs.
Since 1945, the widest possible opportunity has been given to study the proposal for universal pensions without a means test which the federal government at that time offered to the provinces.
10942	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment
A little further on in his speech the hon. gentleman said:
The fact that after an exhaustive study all parties, and subsequently all provincial governments, unanimously rallied to the support of the universal means-test-free pension plan originally offered by the federal government in 1945 is, I believe, the surest and soundest endorsement that any legislative proposal could hope to have.
They are interesting words, Mr. Speaker. The minister seems to refute them today, as do the members of his party.
Then the hon. gentleman continued as follows:
We have come to the conclusion, after the most careful study of all phases of the problem, that the so-called "universal pay-as-you-go" system of old age security, financed by special contributions into a fund established especially for the purpose, is the system most likely to meet the needs of our aged population 70 years and over, both now and in the future.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, at that time the minister did not have the ability to see into the future, though in view of the party he represents that would be a most difficult thing to do.
Then, as reported at page 382 of Hansard, the minister went on:
-benefits will in all cases be provided as a matter of right, without any form of means test.
At the same page this very interesting statement is recorded:
There will be no provisions of any kind for subsequent recovery out of the estate of a deceased pensioner, nor for any liens to be placed against his property.
Two of the provisions in the bill before the house today cause me to wonder what they mean. Do they mean that some old age pensioner will be hauled into court because he made a mistake in assessing his income? The minister says that there is no means test in this bill. As a matter of fact, as reported at page 10896 of Hansard, he said:
They-
Referring to the old age pensioners.
-will not suffer any indignity, if this can be called an indignity, and I do not think it is. They will not be asked to do anything that a corporation president is not asked to do, or any other person in the country, in the way of providing information with respect to income or having the accuracy of that return checked.
Is that a valid statement, Mr. Speaker? Does the minister mean to tell me that there are corporation presidents who are going to fill out a form asking for more money and which they will have to show to somebody else? How many corporation presidents does

DEBATES	December 9, 1966
the minister know who actually show their income tax returns to people other than those in the income tax branch or their accountant? How many corporation presidents will be affected by the provisions of this bill, in addition to the provisions for fraud contained in the Income Tax Act, which take care of those unfortunate receipients of the old age pension who may make a mistake or perhaps inadvertently submit a wrong return? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the statement the pensioners will not be asked to do anything anybody else is not asked to do is completely at variance with the facts as we in this house know them.
I do not care whether you call it an income test, a needs test or a means test, Mr. Speaker. The application of the test can vary, but the change is a semantic one only. There is no difference in fact between the provisions of this bill and a means test. The provisions of this bill constitute a means test. A means test is imposed as soon as some measure of a person's income is used to determine whether or not he or she qualifies for additional benefit. No matter what the minister and other hon. members on that side of the house say, this is the fact of the matter.
I heard the minister taking the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) to task in his speech yesterday. He questioned her facts as they related to the amount required today for a minimum standard for our old age pensioners. It seems to me that the minister does not read his mail. I want to refer him to a letter written by the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), and incidentally to all members of parliament as well.
This letter is signed by the president, Mr. Nathan W. Medd and Mrs. Marian Goddard, secretary of this federation which represents, as the minister knows, the great majority of the pensioners in this country today.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The letter reads:
Whereas: A recent survey shows cost of living to be approximately $138 per month,-
I am not taking this from the Globe and Mail. I notice the minister does not like to get things from the Globe and Mail. The hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) does, but then divisions in the minister's party are not unusual.
Whereas: A recent survey shows cost of living to be approximately $138 per month,

-Our senior citizens need more than the $105 per month for a decent standard of living, and with the straight $100 per month they would be encouraged to earn the extra needed, if able to do so, which would be an economic advantage to any country.
The minister has received this letter. He knows what it says. He received many more. On November 3 he got one from the Toronto Area Retired Workers Council. They took a survey at the Canadian National Exhibition, one part of which is as follows:
Do you believe the basic old age security pension should be increased from $75 to $100 and without a means test?
Ninety per cent of those asked said yes. Who are the other 10 per cent? Liberal voters in that area, no doubt. They are followers of the minister and his philosophy.

Perhaps I can see the future a little more clearly than other people. Nevertheless, who are hon. members opposite to accuse us of using this measure as a political football, in view of the number of times we have asked this government to increase the old age pension across the board because the need for such action is now. The minister has the colossal affrontery to suggest that we are using this as a political football when he makes crass political statements.
Let me refer to this communication from the Senior Women's Committee for Pension Increase of January 10, 1966. This was a telegram sent to the Prime Minister, and in one part it reads:
The Senior Women's Committee for Pension Increase strongly urges you to increase the Old Age Pension to $100 per month at 65. High cost of living, especially drugs and rent makes food and clothing impossible. All other pensions and allowances have been raised. $100 per month would give a good and regular boost to industry and comfort the elderly people.
They added another little point which I shall quote, because I would not want to be thought political:
Result of election indicates concern of people.
Old Age Security Act Amendment
These are people who represent the old age pensioners of our country. Who in this house has not received hundreds of communications from old age pensioners in his constituency asking for $100 a month across the board without any means test and without any semantic change by the government.
I will read a communication which I think is a good example of the sort of thing we have all been getting. The letter is dated March 8, 1966, and it is from a pensioner. It reads:
Dear Sir,
I am a pensioner aged 74, living at 535-10th St. E., Saskatoon. My sole means of support is the federal old age pension and provincial supplement totalling $81.50.
The cost of living is now so high as well as the cost of rent for my single room that I find it almost impossible to live, and keep everything paid for.
I hope that you will take the situation of people like myself under advisement, and I suggest that $25 per month in addition to what I am now getting would make life much more bearable.

That is a typical comment from one who will never be in the position to test whether his party would make a good or bad government.
I read from page 393 of Hansard:
I can give reasons why the committee recommended universal payments. First, It was felt that in the case of those who did not need the payments it would be a simple matter for the Minister of Finance if he so chose to draw them back in the way of taxes.
Almost every member in this house knows that is true. The minister, however, does not seem to think that is true, neither does the hon. member for Verdun.
In the second place, it was thought that the administrative problem would be considerable.
10944	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment
The minister, I am sure, is aware of the work done in this committee as it looked into every facet of the problem. The minister might be interested to read the Journals of the House of Commons for 1950 which deal with the matter.
I continue quoting:
It does not matter what figure you choose as the breaking point between those who will receive and those who will not; you are applying a means test. It may be that it would be an infinitely more generous means test than that which had prevailed hitherto,-
Those words seem applicable today.
-but nevertheless it would involve the application of such a test. That in turn would have brought with it almost all the obiectional features of the present administration of the means test. It would mean that you would be penalizing thrift in many cases while making payments in other cases to those who have not generally practised equal thrift.
If the minister refers to yesterday's Hansard, to the excellent speech of the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Regimbal), he will see some interesting facts. If a person earns an extra $60 a month he receives nothing. If he receives, let us say, $58 a month he receives a cheque for 50 cents every month from the government of Canada. Is that not wonderful? It will cost the government $1.50 to send the cheque. It will cost the taxpayers $2, and the aged person will receive 50 cents. Many pensioners in this country I am sure will frame such a cheque, hang it on the wall, and do without an extra slice of bread.
It would have meant more intrusions on the part of officials into the affairs of individuals.
That is still true today:
For these and other very good reasons, not least of all being the administrative difficulty of enforcing such a test as compared with the administrative ease with which money could be taken back in taxes from those who did not need it, the committee arrived, I think soundly, at the conclusion that the simplest and most effective system was the universal system.
Those words were uttered 15 years ago and are as applicable today as they were then. They were accepted by the government of that day with approbation. Had the hon. member for Verdun been here then he too, would have approved of them with everything else he approved of today in his speech.
The problem is serious. I do not know if the minister realizes the seriousness to the people of Canada of his proposal.

Had these two groups formed part of the total, the 54 per cent figure would undoubtedly be higher. For all persons who were included the median income was $960: $1,440 for men and $830 for women.
Fifty nine per cent of Canada's older people in 1961 were members of families as defined by the census. If the husband and wife are still together, which was true in 80 per cent of such families, the wife may have had an income as well as the husband, and unmarried children, if present in the home, may have been making some contribution in support of their parents. The latest information is from a D.B.S. survey in 1958 which shows that non-farm families with heads aged 65 and over had more liquid assets and less debts than families generally. For most people in both groups, however, the amounts involved were small: 60 per cent of the older families, and 80 per cent of all families had liquid assets of less than $2,000; and 96 per cent of the former, as compared with 88 per cent of the latter, had consumer debts of less than $1,000.
It is probably true in Canada, as in the United States and Great Britain, that the most important capital owners among the aged are a small minority of the total group. This same 1958 survey shows that for the group aged 65 and over, 15.3 per cent of family units with incomes of $5,000 and more held 40.3 per cent of the liquid assets of the group. Similarly in the United States in 1960, the top 20 per cent of the age group 65 years and over, ranked by size of income, held about 50 per cent of the liquid assets.
I might also refer to the number of homes that these people owned and occupied. On page 14 of the report it is stated:
Owned homes are the principal asset that people bring with them into old age. In 1961, of 747,000 dwellings occupied by households, whose head was aged 65 and over, 77 per cent were owner-occupied. In the spring of 1959 it was estimated that over 90 per cent of home owners aged 65 and over owned their homes, mortgage-free. This means, of course, that a modest cash outlay enabled such families to remain in their own homes. However, as pointed out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in its submission to the Senate committee, the quality of the housing stock occupied by the elderly is much below average.
The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) referred to the fact that these people had experienced two wars and a depression and had attempted to rear families during that time. They have suffered from a lack of educational training and job opportunities, so is it any wonder that the Senate report gives an indication of the low level of income that these people have experienced over the years?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare spoke last night he was quite sensitive about the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) that elderly persons need $138.96 a month to live on. This amount was culled from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail in connection with a conference on aging held on January 28 of this year. For the
December 9, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment benefit of the minister I think I should put on record part of this article:
An elderly person living alone needs a monthly income of at least $138.96, a committee of the Canadian Conference on Aging decided yesterday.
A sample budget for elderly persons was prepared by the committee and will be forwarded to the Canadian Welfare Council as a possible guide for planning future needs.
The group, headed by Gerard Nepveu, director-general of Quebec's Family and Social Welfare Department, agreed that two items in the budget, housing and health care, fluctuate from individual to individual and from region to region.
Some members also protested the sum set aside for recreation and leisure, $6, was too low.
The budget, for an elderly person living alone allowed $36.91 for food; $50 for housing which included heat and a refrigerator and stove; $2.16 for utilities such as electricity; $6.25 for household and personal supplies such as soap, toothpaste and services to keep the home operating; $3.24 for furniture on the assumption the furniture has been paid for and no major replacement is needed; $7.08 for clothing and its care; $6 for transportation which, budget presenter Agnes Higgins of Montreal said, would allow six outings a week in some areas; $12 for health care excluding drugs; $6 for leisure and recreation; $8.02 for reading, telephone and personal allowance and $1.30 for gifts and contributions including church collections.
Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that church receipts are down when the old age pensioners are committed to $1.30 a month?
This is the first budget for the elderly on a national scale. It was based partly on projected figures for 1963 and 1964 on personal expenditures on consumer goods and services per capita per month and partly on information supplied by experts from various regions.
Several committee members said they hoped a copy would be sent to provincial governments and to departments of welfare.
Budgets have been prepared, however, on regional or local basis. Last October, the social planning council of metropolitan Toronto told the Ontario government's select committee on aging that a single elderly woman needs about $118 a month, a single retired man $126 and an elderly couple $213.
The national budget, described as modest but adequate, allowed $223.82 for a retired couple. Mrs. Higgins said a housewife can save money by buying in larger quantities so the food costs were not necessarily doubled. She allowed rent for a one-bedroom apartment at $73, although rent for such shelter varies from $60 to $90. Most of the items such as utilities, household supplies, clothing, health care and gifts were seen as being about twice as expensive for two as one but transportation and recreation were increased only about 40 per cent because one person may stay at home more than the other-
Several committee members said they would have liked a more generous budget but that the sample one should be satisfactory for those who have resources other than the old age security benefits.
They refrained from asking the Canadian Welfare Council to implement the budget but asked that it be used as a sample and updated as the living costs vary.

This was the statement, Mr. Speaker, cited by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and about which the minister became very sensitive. I would imagine he is entitled to become sensitive because he also received a communique from the Canadian Welfare Council prepared by the executive director of the council, Reuben C. Baetz. In referring to the proposed guaranteed income plan of the government Mr. Baetz stated:
One of the main purposes of the study is to gather more reliable data for establishing adequate public social security provisions, not only for those receiving assistance under current programs, but also for those who would be included in any new programs.
Up to now, decisions on benefits have been determined by a combination of political expediency, financial limitations, and rough estimates of need. For example, the federal government's program for a guaranteed minimum income for the aged is being launched without a thorough study of minimum needs, as was recommended by the special committee of the Senate on aging.
I think this is one of the main points, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has neglected. What he should have done was this. When the house reconvened in September and we were told that medicare would be delayed for one year, he should have brought in his legislation in regard to pensions and referred the subject matter to a special committee to study the needs of our senior citizens. That committee would have had before it specialists in the needs and requirements of senior citizens. But what did he do? The minister waited until December before bringing forward his proposed legislation, sandwiched it in with medicare, and he is now attempting to pressure it through the house.
The Senate report lists the recommendations the minister is proposing to follow and sets forth the need for the creation of a competent body to ascertain the income requirements of older people so as to develop a socially acceptable budget for single persons and couples which would be adjusted automatically annually on the basis of a suitable index of consumer spending of earnings, with a review every five years to reflect changes in the relative circumstances of the working population and the retired population.
The committee suggested an amount of $1,260 per year for single persons and outlined the procedure, which the minister is now attempting to follow by saying that he will require a simplified form which will disclose a person's income. It is also noteworthy that the committee indicated there would be sample
December 9, 1986	COMMONS
checks made periodically, as under unemployment insurance, with no means or needs test inquiries along traditional lines. This is the formula which the minister has adopted, with one exception, and that is that the Senate committee on aging reported that the eligible age for receipt of the pension should be 65. That recommendation has not been followed by the minister.

speechtext:
Yes, I am very well aware of that, but I think the minister has used the Senate report as the basis of his formula for developing the guaranteed annual income. One might ask, Mr. Speaker, what are the restrictions with regard to this guaranteed income program? First of all, it restricts many senior citizens from working because of the financial disadvantage in obtaining the supplemental income. As has been said, not many people would be happy to work knowing that if they earned over $60 they would be deprived of the supplementary income. When they earn less than $60 the supplementary income is reduced by $1 for every $2 they earn. That is the first point. The second point is that there are insurmountable difficulties in filling out the required forms.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The minister nonchalantly referred to the ease of filling these forms. I refer him to clause 9 of the proposed bill which, under the heading "Calculation of Income", says:
For the purposes of this Part,
(a) the income for a year of a person, other than a person described in paragraph (b), in his income for that year computed in accordance with the Income Tax Act, minus-
Certain allowances.
Also set forth is the provision with regard to the calculation of income for spouses.
I have looked at the Income Tax Act to see how clearly income is defined. I notice that from pages 5 to 13 the Income Tax Act sets out what income is. At page 14 it determines amounts not to be included in the computing of income, from pages 15 to 19 it sets out deductions, from pages 29 to 33 it shows deductions not allowed in the computing of income, and from pages 33 to 40 it sets out miscellaneous rules for computing income. The minister, as can be seen, has not set the old age pensioners an easy task in determining what their income is. The minister says
23033-693J
Old Age Security Act Amendment that it is simply a matter of filling out a form. He will, first of all, have to inform pensioners as to what constitutes income. I venture to say that any pamphlet sent to a pensioner will have ten pages at least devoted to setting out what constitutes income under the Income Tax Act.
Let us take an example of how this will work. For a person to be entitled to the supplement he must file a statement showing his previous year's income. In other words, a person filling out the form in 1967 will have to show his income in 1966. Does the minister suppose that an old age pensioner who has done babysitting to supplement her income will keep an accurate record of what she has earned over the year?
Take as an example the difficulty of calculating incomes for other people. The Senate report on aging shows that over 500,000 pensioners own their own homes. Many of these home owners rent rooms to supplement their incomes. How does an old age pensioner determine the income from rented rooms? He must take the gross income, then take into account the allowance for depreciation of the building, the proportionate allowance for heating, the proportionate allowances for realty taxes, repairs and so on. It is not easy for an old age pensioner to determine the income derived from renting rooms.
Let us take into account that many pensioners have sold their homes and are living off mortgages they have obtained in selling their homes. Most mortgages these days call for, blended payments of principal and interest. Principal and interest are not separated as they were in the past. Can you imagine an old age pensioner who gets $75 per month on a mortgage trying to calculate how much of that $75 is principal and how much is interest? That presents an almost insurmountable difficulty.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has kept quiet about the options that old age pensioners have under this bill. I expect the reason is that the minister appreciates the difficulties I have referred to and the difficulties in determining what pensioners need. When the old age pensioners get a synopsis of that part of the bill dealing with options and elections they will be as confused as we all are. Let me suggest an easy solution to the problem of filling out forms. I think all members of parliament should have imposed on them the task of filling out these forms that old age pensioners will have to fill out. After most members have filled out 10, 15 or 20
December 9, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment forms they will come back and say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, For goodness sake, apply the principle of universality to this problem and avoid all the complications and administrative difficulties that otherwise ensue. An hon. member beside me says that we also ought to avoid all expenses which may otherwise result.
Can you imagine the difficult task that an old age pensioner will have in filling out a form? We do not know at the moment whether the minister will include the provision contained in other forms, such as the ones having to do with veterans allowances, that the truth of the information contained in the document shall be attested to in the presence of a notary public, minister or some other person in authority. Can you imagine somebody swearing that the declared earnings for the previous year are the actual and true amount? Difficult as such a computation is, to be forced to make such a declaration will be a humiliating experience. Also, in clause 20 of the bill the minister sets out the penalty provisions in new section 21. The word used in that clause is "knowingly". That may be an escape for some people because many people would not knowingly fill out the form improperly. In any event, the clause reads:
(1) Every person who
(a) knowingly makes a false or misleading statement in any application or statement required or permitted by this Act or makes any such application or statement that by reason of any nondisclosure of facts is false or misleading or obtains any benefit payment by false pretences- is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
The bill does not say what the punishment is, but under the old act any person found guilty was liable to a fine of $500 or six months imprisonment or to both fine and imprisonment.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Maybe the minister is going to tell us what it constitutes. If I remember correctly, in the absence of any provision set forth in the Summary Convictions Act those are the limits, $500 or six months, or both fine and imprisonment. Can you imagine an old age pensioner being confronted with this type of provision? What a position to put a person in.
Another point is that the guaranteed annual income plan set forth by the minister is based on past income and not on present needs. May I give an example. If an old age pensioner has made sufficient money in the year 1966 he will not be entitled to the pension in 1967. But suppose in 1967 he runs into


a serious illness, as a result of which his savings are depleted and his assets are reduced. That is the time of actual need. This is why we are so insistent that we get away from this means test and that there should be a lump sum increase for these people. A person who in 1967 suffers such a depletion of income and reduction of assets will have to wait until 1968 before he can get any benefit under this bill. Is this the type of help we want to give our senior citizens?
One further point is that the present act does not cover people from the age of 65 to 68. The minister may say that those who are in need can apply for old age assistance in the provinces in which they live. But the minister knows as well as I do that under the Old Age Assistance Act the basis in Ontario under the Canada Assistance Plan is need, but it is need coupled with the severe means test embracing the ten items described yesterday. I would point out that the agreement with regard to the regulations in Ontario has not been signed and therefore people in this category are not getting assistance on the basis of need. We have been promised for months that this agreement would be entered into but to date no such agreement has been effected.
Yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) said:
Estimates in the current year are that the guaranteed income supplement will cost between $260 million and $280 million in its first year. Take the median figure of $270 million; this is $100 million less than the cost of a $25 a month increase in the flat rate pension. The cost of the flat rate pension, of course, would increase annually so that by 1970 it would amount to something in the neighbourhood of $200 million a year more than the guaranteed income supplement.
Then he went on to put a nice sentence in the latter part of his statement:
It is proposed that the payments for this income supplement will be financed from the old age security fund. The tax measures required in connection with these expenditures will be dealt with by the Minister of Finance in his budget in the very near future.
The Minister of Finance is going to introduce an additional tax to take care of these problems with regard to the old age security fund. I feel certain that the Canadian people would gladly pay a slight additional amount if they thought that every old age pensioner would get a flat increase of $25 or $30. I think there is sufficient generosity within Canadian taxpayers that if the money is for the help of senior citizens they will certainly pay it. I believe that the minister should give effect to this argument and make sure that there is a
December 9, 19G6	COMMONS
flat rate increase for all Canada's senior citizens.
Yesterday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) jumped up when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was speaking and asked, "Where are you going to get the money?" The hon. member said, from savings in defence expenditures. This is one source where we could get it but another source is the increased productivity that we, I hope, are going to enjoy within the next few years. With that increased productivity, surely senior citizens who have contributed in the past should enjoy the fruits of the present. This is one source to which the Minister of Finance should direct his attention if he has any real concern for pensioners.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare also spoke about an appeal board. He said that there has always been an appeal board and that it is nothing new. But it is new in the sense that it is going to deal with people who appeal against the department's questioning of the amount of income they have shown in filing their forms. Can you, Mr. Speaker, imagine a person in a small centre in your riding, attempting to process an appeal? Can you imagine an old age pensioner, 67 years or over, going before an appeal board? How many appeal boards are going to be established? Will an old age pensioner have to travel 30 or 40 miles to present his case? Do you notice, Mr. Speaker, that the final clause in that provision says that the appeal board's decision shall be binding?
I would say that the plan the minister has set forth creates two classes of senior citizens categorized on the basis of income, those who have income and those who do not. What a terrible indictment of our senior citizens in view of their contribution in past years. Second, this plan will sow discord and ill feeling among pensioners. One pensioner will be asking another pensioner, "How much did you get," and when he finds out that the other is getting more he will go home and ask, "Why does he get so much and I do not get the same? He is not declaring all his income." Ill feeling will be generated.
Again I say that the bill is terribly complex from the point of view of administration. The plan runs against a proper structuring of a feasible pension combining an adequate income with decency and respect. We in the N.D.P. say that senior citizens should be given at least three things, first, proper housing, second, an adequate health plan and, third, an adequate income so that they will be able to
Old Age Security Act Amendment live decently and happily. Mr. Speaker, I can almost hear our senior citizens, when they receive this great form and the 20-page pamphlet that will go with it, giving three cheers for the Minister of National Health and Welfare-Scrooge, Scrooge, Scrooge.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, judging from recent experience on welfare measures in this house I do not think it is going to be possible to convince the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) and the government of the error of their ways with respect to the legislation now before us.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
However, on this quiet Friday afternoon I should like to take the opportunity to repeat a theme with which I have dealt on many occasions when welfare measures have been before parliament. I refer to the urgent necessity to bring about a more co-ordinated and integrated approach to welfare services. During the past three years we have spent a good deal of time in the House of Commons dealing with welfare measures. I think it is a fair conclusion to reach that we are no closer than we were to the achievement of a coordinated approach in dealing with what is one of the basic problems in the modern state, the problem of the social and economic needs of individuals in our industrialized technological civilization. Indeed, we have moved farther from the desired goal rather than closer to the approach which has been recommended by experts in the field, by the provincial governments which have the final responsibility for welfare measures, by social workers' associations, by the Canadian Welfare Council, and particularly by Mr. John Morgan who formerly was associated with the Toronto school of social work.
Today we have another example of a government which suffers by following a hit-and-miss approach in dealing with welfare problems rather than trying to establish an over-all comprehensive scheme. Some hon. members who are here now will recall that in 1962 parliament did move to establish this greatly to be desired integrated approach. A bill establishing a dominion welfare council, which was designed to be the counterpart of the national health council, was passed. Unfortunately that bill never was implemented. This is one of the main reasons that over the past three years we have been endeavouring to deal with urgent welfare measures, especially pension matters and the question of
December 9, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment security for our senior citizens, on this piecemeal basis. This was the basic problem which arose in connection with the Canada Pension Plan. The basic criticism of the medicare scheme with which we dealt a few days ago was the failure to integrate and tie together the various aspects of the social welfare needs of Canada at the present time.
Many hon. members who have spoken before me in this debate have pointed out the inadequacies of the legislation before us. For example, it has been mentioned that it is reaching us too late. The need for an increase in old age security payments has existed in Canada for at least a year. It is an obvious need arising from rampant inflation which has affected the economy of Canada during the past 12 months. Any member of this house who is in touch with his constituents will be aware that this is the number one issue in the field of welfare. It was for this reason that we failed to understand why the government was giving priority to the medicare scheme when it would not be implemented until July, 1968.
My correspondence, and I am sure the correspondence of other members of the house, has dealt with the growing gap in respect oi the old age security payments caused by the continuing process of inflation and particularly in respect of the high cost of food which is felt most keenly by our senior citizens. Obviously the government has been aware ol this situation because the committee on consumer credit has been dealing with this matter. Certainly it has been brought to our attention by the protest groups which have risen spontaneously across the country during the past few months. The bill before us deals with the matter too late and deals with the problem in the wrong way. It is not at all adequate to deal with it. As has been pointed out, it applies only to the recipients of old age security. It provides no benefit at all for those in the most needy group, the recipients of old age assistance. As a matter of fact their needs are pretty well taken care of by existing provincial schemes.
For the past four or five years in the province of Manitoba there has been a system of supplementary payments which is based on precisely the same formula which is defended by this government and referred to as an income maintenance scheme. It has provided those people who are in receipt of old age assistance pensions with supplementary benefits, although it is referred to as involving a


needs test in contrast to the outmoded means test.
The scheme which is before us this afternoon is not a new concept in the field of pension payments or in the field of dealing with the matter of inadequate income for recipients of old age pensions. It is borrowed directly from provinces such as the province of Manitoba which have already pioneered in this field. While the minister has indicated that this plan will in no way interfere with the supplementary benefits paid under existing provincial schemes, I am sure he will find that the scheme proposed here will be substituted by the provincial governments for the schemes they already have been operating over the past number of years.
The basic criticism I make of the proposal is that it is a backward step in respect of welfare principles in the modern state. I am aware that the Canadian Welfare Council attempts to co-ordinate the various functions and activities of the voluntary groups across the country, but I believe that if there had been a national welfare council to make recommendations in the field of policy the government would have avoided the retrograde step that is being taken in the measure before us in respect of the principle involved. No matter how hard the government tries to explain that this is a progressive step and a forward move in the field of welfare, it cannot deny the fact that this is a return to the charity concept of the 1930's.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Canada was late in coming to grips with the social problems of the modern state. We were late in coming to grips with these problems because we were basically an agrarian society up until the last 10 or 20 years. Our first welfare measures did not even borrow principles from the modern concepts of welfare which had been established in the United Kingdom, countries in Europe and the United States, because our programs were geared almost exclusively to the charity concept.
The program of income maintenance, as it is euphemistically referred to by the minister, will re-establish one of the difficulties which parliament tried to remove when it adopted the principle of universality in 1951. That principle was a new break-through in our attitude toward pensions for senior citizens. This so-called income maintenance program will aggravate one of the social problems we have been trying to avoid in recent years. It will discourage our older citizens from taking advantage of job opportunities which arise from
December 9, 1966

time to time. In other words, it will perpetuate a problem which has created one of the main drawbacks in regard to war veterans allowances.
Anyone who has had experience in administering war veterans allowances in recent years will appreciate that an attempt has been made to move away from the basic drawbacks of that program, the criteria which discourage veterans from supplementing their war veterans allowance incomes. This encourages slothfulness rather than initiative on the part of pensioners to supplement their incomes by taking on casual work. This difficulty is being perpetuated by this legislation at a time when we are trying to solve a problem in relation to the increasing percentage of our citizens who are in the senior citizen age bracket. With modern health and hospitalization care facilities more and more of our citizens are living beyond the proverbial three score and ten years. Experts in the field of health and welfare have been trying to advance the idea that rather than discouraging the use of skills acquired over a lifetime of experience we should be devising plans to provide ways and means of helping our senior citizens to maintain their position, perhaps in a restricted way, in the world of work so that these skills can be used to fill the gap in this period of Canada's development.
Quite obviously the principle of income maintenance as embodied in the bill will completely discourage any positive effort on the part of recipients of old age security to supplement their incomes by casual work because any additional income will result in a loss of additional benefit. This problem has been solved in respect of war veterans allowances by ignoring casual earnings and by allowing a certain time period during a year when additional earnings can be made by a recipient of war veterans allowances without interfering with his income from that source. There is no similar provision in this bill as I read it. Perhaps this is an oversight, but I think it is fair on this basis to argue that this is a retrograde step and to point out to the government that it is running against new concepts regarding the occupational positions of senior citizens in the modem state.
The government's philosophy in respect of this measure is similar to the philosophy often adopted by members of the Liberal party toward the field of welfare. I recall the agitation in 1957 when the Liberal government of that day decided to increase old age security payments by $6 per month, those of us who were

Old Age Security Act Amendment active in public life in 1957 will recall the disastrous consequences to the Liberal government which resulted from that attitude toward old age pensions. That move was calculated carefully on the basis of narrow concepts and was motivated by very much the same thinking which is behind the present legislation. I suggest to the minister and the government that rather than removing the agitation which has been felt by hon. members of the house over the past few months in respect of the income gap facing our senior citizens, this measure will increase that agitation. There is an aspect of camouflage and dissimulation to this bill which will be seen through readily by our senior citizens.
It is my belief that our senior citizens, particularly those who have been supplementing their incomes and thereby providing some useful service in their declining years, will realize quickly that they will receive nothing more after this plan is put into effect than they now receive under provincial schemes. Those who have been supplementing their incomes by casual employment will find that after the implementation of this plan they will not benefit from its provisions because to do so they will have to give up their casual work and earnings.
In recent years welfare workers have been endeavouring to make use of the creative ability and capacity of older persons under the principles that were established by the Old Age Security Act. The principle of universality recognized the fact that the earning capacity of these individuals is not as great as it was and that a basic income had to be provided without discouraging the useful participation of a pensioner in the contemporary work world.
The fundamental point I wish to make this afternoon is that this bill takes a backward and retrograde step in our efforts to deal with income maintenance for our senior citizens.
I have referred to the experience of the government with reference to war veterans allowance and how it got around this difficulty. In respect of the present legislation the government is falling right back into the policy that was abandoned under war veterans allowance.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
There is another aspect of the legislation that deserves to be criticized. Nothing specific has been said in this regard but it has been indicated that this measure will require special taxation to provide the funds necessary. This argument has been used by the Minister
December 9, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment of Finance (Mr. Sharp) as an excuse for introducing what has been variously called a minibudget, a baby budget and even a miniscule budget. We do not know when the minibudget will be presented. It was supposed to come in the latter part of November or early December. It was supposed to be tied in specifically with the increased costs that would arise from the implementation of this measure to assist our old age pension recipients. Here again we have violated the principle that was established in the excellent legislation of 1951.
That legislation was hailed as a major break-through in social policy. All of us who were in the house at that time accepted the new principle as being a desirable one in the modern state. There was to be established a special old age security fund. This was to deal with all the changing needs over the years, because nothing is static in society in the field of welfare payments. But now we are going off on another ad hoc tangent. Notwithstanding the advice received by the government and the obvious need for co-ordination and cooperation in this field, we are specifically earmarking a new budget and tying it to the fiscal needs that will be generated by this legislation. It ignores, too, the fact that need has been created by runaway inflation. I suppose it would be possible to argue that part of the runaway inflation has been created by the on-again, off-again fiscal policies of the government. The "Gordon" concept and the "Sharp" concept of fiscal policies seem to be diametrically opposed. With succeeding ministers of finance espousing different philosophies with regard to fiscal policies, it is quite understandable that in recent months inflation has tended to get out of control.
Even the government's venture into the new pension area of the Canada Pension Plan, with its increase in taxation of course, has had a significant effect on the cost of living in this country. I agree with those who have already spoken in this debate and pointed out that the government has been largely responsible for creating its own problem. In trying to solve the problem it is putting the finger directly on the group of senior citizens and saying: If we pay you this additional sum of money, we will have to raise taxes.
That is hardly a fair diagnosis, particularly when you have a scheme that in many respects is a camouflaged approach to the problem because it is dealing with an area of need that is already substantially covered by policies of social assistance based on a needs test

which have been established in the provinces across the country.
If the government had accepted the advice that has reached them from time to time from this side of the house, the present scheme would be quite unnecessary. I agree completely with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatter ton), who tried to persuade the government along these lines when we were discussing the Canada Pension Plan, that the old age security program is an excellent one, a program that fits perfectly into the modern framework of social welfare policy. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich made the point that we could have handled the need for increasing pension benefits to the important, growing segment of our senior citizens if we had worked through the legislative machinery already provided in the Old Age Security Act. But the government ignored that advice. The same advice has been given during this discussion.
We can deal with the problem, as the hon. member pointed out-this is the viewpoint of most of the members of the opposition so far as I can gather after listening to the speeches-by raising the financial benefit to $100 a month and providing payment for the program through the existing social security fund, without imposing any stigma on our senior citizens and without discouraging them from using their skills in the area of the Canadian economy which today urgently needs the skills that are theirs. This program could be carried out much more simply and much more effectively and would represent a step forward rather than a retrograde step as I am convinced is involved in the bill now before us.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
As I said in my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I do not expect that any of us, no matter how long we discuss this theme, will be able to convince the minister of the error of his ways. I am certainly not going to prolong my remarks this afternoon because there are others who want at least to attempt to make the minister see the error of his ways in this respect. We are into the eleventh month of a long session of parliament. One of the reasons our sessions are stretching out in ever-lengthening proportions in recent years is the haphazard approach of the government in dealing with welfare measures. Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of Bill C-251, not just nominal support by as vigorous support as I can offer for what I consider to be the most progressive piece of legislation this house has seen during my brief sojourn here.
I cannot stress too forcibly the need for this legislation, a need which has been brought to my attention time and time again by people in my riding and I am sure is felt as strongly across the country. This bill, viewed objectively, is not only a resourceful bill but a humanitarian one designed to meet a very immediate need, It is always disappointing to note the regularity with which the opposition tends to treat bills, regardless of the subject matter with which they deal or their merit, as being inadequate, ill conceived or governed by considerations other than the best ones that should be used for promulgating such legislation.
It seems to me that one of the most important features of this bill, which I hope in time will become more obvious to members of the opposition, is that it will probably end the shameless bartering which goes on amongst political parties at election time for the support of senior citizens. This bill is not so much governed by that consideration as by an assessment of the particular needs of senior citizens. It is the consideration of need more than any other that will in the future, as a result of this bill, govern the attitude of political parties to the problem of the financial needs of senior citizens.
In his remarks the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) suggested that we did not really understand the problem of the needs of senior citizens. I cannot remember exactly whether he suggested therefore that we should not do anything precipitously. However, if that is a fair interpretation of what he said I might suggest to him that we know enough about the particular needs at this point in time to say unequivocally and categorically that this bill is necessary. It seems to me to be pious to simply suggest that it is not as perfect as it might be. I am sure that even the minister might admit that no piece of legislation in its entirely is absolutely perfect, but this is one of the very best and most progressive pieces of legislation this
Old Age Security Act Amendment house has seen in a long time and indisputably it meets a need. I defy any member opposite to prove to me in language not polemical and rhetorical but on the basis of straight analysis, that this bill does not in fact meet an immediate and pressing need. I have not yet heard anything from the other side that would suggest that this bill does not meet an immediate pressing need.

This was a fair appeal not only because in substance he could document and prove the distinction-it takes a very short-sighed individual who, having read the minister's speech, does not see the distinction -but also because the appeal had merit on the following grounds which are most important. There is not a shadow of doubt that the spectre of a means test is a frightening prospect to the senior citizens of this country. It is not very difficult for hon. members opposite, for reasons best known to themselves, to raise that spectre and insist that the government is trying to lead the senior ciiizens down the garden path. To argue that it is a beguiling piece of eloquence to try to draw a distinction between a needs test and a means test is wrong; yet it is perfectly possible for hon. members opposite to do that. They know they can do it but, as I say, it is a grave abrogation of responsibility to insist that there is in fact no distinction between a needs test and a means test when the truth is that the distinction is unequivocal. If the needs test, as laid

speechtext:
I am not indisposed to giving passage to the bill because on the surface it is a reasonable request, but I think that the house should look at one aspect of this matter. As I understand it, the original authority given to the company to build a line in this area was given in 1947, presumably for a ten year period. In 1956 the time limit for constructing the line was again extended for another ten years, which I gather expires on May 14 next. We are now being asked to grant another ten year extension, bringing the expiry date to May 14, 1977, which will be 30 years from the date the original authority was given to the company.
If I understood correctly what the hon. member for Saguenay (Mr. Blouin) said, the company has operated a railway between Schefferville and Sept-iles since 1954, and there are 282 miles of railway to be constructed between Schefferville and Ungava but there is no construction in that area at the moment. In other words, since the company was given authority by parliament in 1947 to extend the railway into Ungava it has only built the line as far as Schefferville, and that was in 1954. During the last 12 years no construction whatever has been undertaken north from Schefferville to Ungava bay.
The company now comes to parliament requesting another ten year extension, having exhibited not very much interest in extending the railway during the last 12 years. This causes me to take another look at whether or not we should pass this bill, thus giving the company a further ten year extension.
I only pose this question at this time, Mr. Speaker. I do not think we should delay passage of the bill or defeat it. But I do raise the question of the propriety of parliament being asked to give this company a licence to extend the railway northward from Schefferville in view of the fact that for the last 12 years it has not embarked upon any construction project in connection therewith.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word because I feel much the same as the previous two speakers about this matter. The Ungava line was started by Hollinger Mines, as it was known then. The company later became the Iron Ore Company of Canada. It built this line from Seven Islands to Schefferville, originally intending to extend it to a deep water port which, I assume, is 282 miles north of Schefferville.
We are giving the company a licence to sit on a plan. The situation, should the bill pass, cannot be alleviated even though other factors come into play. The Hollinger people, with associated companies, I assume, asked for the original licence 20 years ago. At that time nobody lived in the part of the country to which the line went. Now there is a large community there, and the aspirations of the community may not coincide with the aspirations of the Iron Ore Company of Canada. If another settlement to the north of the present

one is developed, we will be giving the company by this bill the legal right to tie up the whole area because it may not feel it is to its advantage to build this line. We must keep in mind that this company is not in the railroad business and is not interested in railroading as such. It is interested in transportation facilities to haul its products to Seven Islands.
The committee will have to consider passenger services, as well as other facilities in the area. Friends of mine working in the area say that the price of transporting commodities to the area is exorbitantly high. That the company would impose heavy charges is possible, because in wishing to carry its own commodities it might wish to discourage the carriage of other commodities and make it as disadvantageous as possible for others to use the facilities. It may be that there will be sleeping cars and a passenger service. In any event, if we allow the company this additional facility there ought to be a liability on the part of the company to treat this rail line as a transportation system rather than just as a means for bringing out its iron ore. All this may be discussed at greater length in committee. We must bear in mind that not only are we giving the company a permit to build but we are giving it a permit not to build, and that permit not to build will prevent anybody else from going into the area should further development take place in that part of Canada.
The Iron Ore Company of Canada really ought to be called the Iron Ore Company of the United States because it is United States controlled. Its interests are not necessarily the same as the interests of any community which may develop in that area. I cannot imagine that we would allow the Canadian National, Canadian Pacific, the Quebec North Shore Railway or anybody else to go in and provide a service which the company did not provide.
The situation which developed one or two years ago in Gaspe comes to mind. The Liberal and Conservative parties made a great deal of to-do about a private carrier going into Gaspe. In the end the Canadian National was asked to extend the service beyond the points serviced by the carrier, the idea being that the Canadian National would use the private carrier's line and then proceed on the Canadian National line built beyond this point. That was a totally unsatisfactory arrangement. Nevertheless, that arrangement is in keeping with the sort of licence being requested here.
